Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender. - Proverbs 19:17

Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible, kept closer to the author’s own Bible where his argument rests on its wording; capitals for God in quotations (He, His) follow the BSB. “You+” marks every plural “you” (the older “ye”); a plain “you” is singular or general.

The Text Opened

Matt 10:41, 42

Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward, and whoever receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man will receive a righteous man’s reward. And if anyone gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones in the name of a disciple, truly I tell you+, he will never lose his reward.

The troubles into which God brings his ministers and people are many and great. Yet they are not more, or greater, than the comforts which he gives them to support and encourage them in their troubles. Take this chapter as an instance, and the sermon of Christ recorded in it, concerning the severe trials into which his church and children would be brought. As each kind of affliction is foretold, a fitting consolation of its own is usually joined to it. So, to establish the hearts of his suffering servants and to encourage those who would help them, he closes his sermon with the words of the text. In them he declares the high regard he had, not only for his ministers and people themselves, but also for those who would give them any relief, or show them kindness for his sake. He assures them: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward,” and “whoever receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man will receive a righteous man’s reward.”

In brief, the words contain a declaration of the great benefit which those bring to themselves who give any relief and help to ministers or other saints. They teach that there is no such way to fill our treasures as by emptying them for God.

To explain the words, I will briefly show you+:

  1. Who is meant here by a prophet, and who by a righteous man.
  2. What is meant by receiving them.
  3. What the reward is which follows on it.

I. For the first: who is meant here by a prophet, and who by a righteous man.

By a prophet our Savior here means not only extraordinary ministers, such as were directly and extraordinarily inspired by the Holy Spirit, or who had extraordinary revelations to foretell things to come, but also ordinary ministers of the word and interpreters of the Scriptures (John 4:44; Rev 11:18).

By righteous men he means his saints, that is, those who show their justification through faith in Christ by their sanctification and the fruits of a good conscience. These the Scripture commonly calls saints.

II. For the second: what is meant by receiving these?

In answer to this, you+ must know that there are two things to which this receiving may refer.

(1.) To the word and message of a minister. So it means listening to and embracing his holy counsel and doctrine.

(2.) To the person of a minister. So it means giving him shelter, or showing him kindness, as is clear from the instance of cold water given to a prophet or righteous man, spoken of in the following verse. Both of these are implied in this phrase, receiving a prophet: that is, receiving his doctrine, by embracing it and submitting to it, and his person, by sheltering, helping and relieving him according to his need.

By receiving a prophet in the name of a prophet is meant helping and relieving him for the sake of his particular calling, eo nomine, because he is a prophet. So receiving a righteous man in the name of a righteous man means the same thing: relieving him for the sake of his general calling, because he is a Christian, a child of God and a member of Christ.

III. For the third particular: what is meant here by the reward of a prophet, and of a righteous man? I answer: these phrases, receiving a prophet’s, and a righteous man’s, reward, may be taken actively or passively. Actively, for the reward which a prophet or a righteous man gives. Passively, for the reward which God gives to the one and to the other. The reward which a prophet gives is, as a minister, to preach the word of reconciliation to those who receive him, as Peter did to Cornelius (Acts 10:34, etc.); to pray for them, as Abraham did for Abimelech (Gen 20:7, 17); and to bless them, as Melchizedek blessed Abraham (Gen 14:19).

The reward which a righteous man gives is, in private, to instruct and edify, to pray for, and to be a good pattern and example of righteousness to those who welcome or otherwise relieve him.

The reward which is given by God to either of these, for the kindness anyone shows to them, is so surpassing and excellent a weight of glory that it cannot be expressed by the tongue of men or angels. Yet it differs in degrees, as is clear from Dan 12:3.

Some take these phrases, receiving a prophet’s and a righteous man’s reward, in the first sense, actively, and others passively. I think they may be taken in both.

The words, explained in this way, give us several points of doctrine.

From the duty expressed here, of receiving and relieving prophets and righteous men, and from the way it is set down, we may observe:

1. Doctrine. All needed help and good hospitality are to be given to ministers of the gospel. This is the main and principal point intended.

2. Doctrine. Christian kindness is to be shown not only to ministers, but also to all the members of Christ. For our blessed Savior is not content to have mentioned a prophet, but also adds a righteous man.

These two sorts make up the household of faith, to whom the apostle urges Christians especially to do good (Gal 6:10).

Question. Is our charity to reach no further?

Answer. Yes, it reaches to all who are in want, but especially to those who have a particular relation to Christ, as his members or ministers, because in them Christ himself is helped and relieved in a special way. So it will be our wisdom to take notice of how far this duty reaches. In all we do, whether for Christians or for others, let us see to it that what we do is done for the Lord’s sake and for conscience’ sake: to the one, in compassion to his members; to the other, in obedience to his will.

3. Doctrine. According to the kindness which we show, so will our reward be. He who receives and relieves a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward. And he who receives and relieves a righteous man will receive the reward of a righteous man.

Verse 42.

And if anyone gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones in the name of a disciple, he will never lose his reward.

Our Savior adds these words to the former to answer beforehand some objections which might be made to them, and also to explain more fully the points mentioned before.

(1.) Objection. It may be put thus: These preachers of the gospel, and those who profess it, are only lowly persons, and little esteemed. What great reward can be expected for welcoming them?

Answer. Little as they are, be they as insignificant and contemptible as the proud world makes them, yet they are not so little in the eyes of the Lord that he will not reward all who are friendly to them.

(2.) Objection. I myself am poor, and can do only a little for them.

Answer. Though your kindness is ever so small, as small as a cup of water, and that cold, taken out of the river without any trouble or cost to heat it, yes, only ONE cupful of it and no more (supposing that to be the most you can do for them), yet it will be rewarded by him who regards the willingness of the giver more than the greatness of the gift.

The greatest difficulty in the words is who are meant here by little ones, for whose sake the reward is promised.

By little ones our Savior means no others than those whom in the verse before he had called prophets and righteous ones.

They are called little ones in two respects:

  1. In regard to the world’s esteem of them.
  2. In regard to their own estimate of themselves.

(1.) First, they are little in the world’s eye. The world, which does not judge according to inward worth, holds them in low esteem. It goes with the servants as it went with their master: they are despised and rejected and trodden underfoot by men. Of old they were called “Desolate” and “Forsaken” (Isa 62:4). In the apostles’ time they were “the scum of the earth, the refuse of the world” (1 Cor 4:13). The experience of all ages confirms as much, and among other ages ours gives no small evidence of it.

The comfort and contentment which God’s people find in the Lord and in the light of his countenance, yes, the hope they have of finding grace in his eyes, make them care less for, and seek less after, the honor, wealth and promotions of the world. And commonly they have only a little of it. Now the world judges according to outward, earthly, worldly glory; it does not discern the spiritual glory of the saints (1 John 3:1).

Do not judge men according to the world’s judgment. Do not think any less of the saints because the world thinks little of them. They are highly favored by the Most High. They are those of whom the world is not worthy; they are the excellent ones (Ps 16:3). But whatever they are in truth, in the eye of the world they are only little ones.

(2.) Secondly, they are little in their own eyes (Gen 18:27). We read how Abraham, speaking to God, calls himself no better than “dust and ashes.” And Jacob confesses himself unworthy, or less than the least of God’s mercies (Gen 32:10).

The reason for this may be that the saints know themselves best. More thoroughly than other men, they search their hearts and observe their ways, and compare themselves with the pure and perfect law of God. They take notice of their inward, secret corruptions as well as of their outward and visible transgressions. In this way they come to know more of themselves than anyone else can know, or even suspect, of them. And this clearer sight of themselves brings them down and lays them low. This is what made Saint Paul cry out, “What a wretched man I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?” (Rom 7:24). This is a mark of true grace and of a sanctified heart. It is the poor in spirit, not the proud in spirit, who are Christ’s blessed ones (Matt 5:3). The false disciple thinks highly of himself. He would be counted not ὁ μικρὸς, a little one, like a true disciple of Christ, but μέγας τὶς, someone great, like Simon Magus (Acts 8:8, 9). This spirit is a satanic spirit. Test your spirit by this mark, whether it is of God or not.

But though all the servants of God are little ones on the account just given, yet there are some among them less than others. In regard to their offices and stations in the church, some are in higher offices and others in lower; some are in office and others not. So also in regard to their abilities and gifts, and graces: some are strong and others are weak; some are the chief of the saints, others the least; some are like the head, and others only like the finger or the foot. And it is probable that the text has the most special regard (and its emphasis is the greater) to the least of all these little ones. So the expression is in Matt 25:40: “Whatever you+ did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you+ did for Me.”

I take notice of this all the more to give Christians a hint: in their charitable gifts, let them have an eye to such ministers or Christians as are more obscure and less regarded in the world. It may be that those of greater worth and note taste deeply of their bounty, since almost everyone has a kindness for them. Meanwhile there may be some poor hidden ones whose worth is less but whose needs are greater. Being low in those gifts or graces which would commend them to more public notice, they are almost buried in forgetfulness. It is true that the more eminent the person who is relieved (caeteris paribus [other things being equal]), the more excellent the work. Yet special care should be taken that the more obscure and least deserving among all who belong to God are not forgotten.

God Takes Notice of the Least of His Saints

The words, explained in this way, give us two special points of doctrine.

1. Doctrine. God takes notice of every one of his saints, even of the least of them, and of kindness shown to them.

Joseph was only a lad, and was sold as a slave. Yet because he was one of the church, one of the little ones, yes, minimorum minimus [the least of the least], God takes notice of him in Egypt, and of the kindness that was shown to him (Gen 39:21). Many other such examples are noted in the Scripture, but none fits our purpose better than the example of Lazarus (Luke 16:20). Though he was a very poor beggar, full of sores, and despised by Dives [the rich man of Luke 16] and all his household, yet God took such notice of him that he made his angels attend him. Yes, God took notice of the kindness which the dogs showed him, for their licking of his sores is recorded for all ages. Note these expressions of the psalmist: “But I am poor and needy; yet the Lord thinks of me” (Ps 40:17). And again: “This poor man called out, and the Lord heard him; He saved him from all his troubles” (Ps 34:6).

Question. If you+ ask why the Lord takes notice of every one of his saints:

Answer 1. They are all his children, and of his household. So, as a tender and careful father and master, he cares for every one. Yes, they are all members of the body of Christ. Now the head takes care of every member, even the least, and takes notice of every kindness done to any of them.

2. Because of the grace in them, they are all like jewels and precious stones. So, as a provident jeweler, he will look after every one of them. Yes, what often appears least may be of greater worth, as a little diamond is of more value than a far greater pebble.

This gives a singular ground of comfort to those who are desolate and forsaken in this world. They may be left alone (as Elijah was, 1 Kgs 19:10), “like a desert owl, like an owl among the ruins,” “like a lone bird on a housetop,” as the psalmist expresses it (Ps 102:6, 7). Yet the Lord is with them and takes care of them. Now if the Lord is with us and takes care of us, what need we fear? How this should encourage us to extend our charity to any one of the saints and members of Christ, though they are lowly and little in the world and not able to repay us! And though no one takes notice of it, let us consider that the Lord takes notice, and will abundantly reward every good work, yes, the least kindness we do to them. Heb 6:10: “God is not unjust. He will not forget your+ work and labor of love which you+ have shown for His name, as you+ have ministered to the saints and continue to do so.” Here God’s not forgetting their labor of love in ministering to the saints implies that, as God takes notice of their kindness, so he is, and always will be, mindful of such persons, to support and help them and do them good in every way.

And if God will remember in this way those who remember the least of his, how will he take it if they are neglected? Beloved, how is it with God’s little ones at this day? Is it not very low with many of them? God takes notice how very low it is. And whether you+ will or not, God will not forsake them. But (to use the words of Mordecai to Esther with some variation, Esth 4:14) if you+ altogether hold back your+ hand at this time, relief will arise for them some other way, but you+ and your+ house (take heed that this word is not fulfilled on you+) will be destroyed. But who knows whether you+ have come to your+ estates for such a time as this!

The Least Kindness Shall Not Lose Its Reward

And so I come to the second and main point of doctrine. It rises from the reward promised to those who show the least kindness to a minister or righteous man: though it is only a cup of cold water, they will never lose their reward. From this we may observe:

2. Doctrine. The least work of charity shown to a minister or righteous man will be abundantly rewarded, and not only hereafter, but here on earth as well.

Our doing good ought to extend to all who are in want and come within the reach of our knowledge and power, as in Gal 6:10: “As we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone.” Yet here I confine my discourse to ministers and righteous ones, because they alone are meant by the little ones mentioned in my text.

That merciful men will be abundantly rewarded hereafter in heaven for their works of charity, there is no doubt, for it is so clearly expressed in the word of God. Luke 16:9: “Make friends for yourselves+ by means of the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when you+ fail, they will receive you+ into eternal dwellings.” And 1 Tim 6:17: “Instruct those who are rich in the present age … to do good, to be rich in good works, and to be generous and ready to share, treasuring up for themselves a firm foundation” for the time to come, that they may lay hold of eternal life.

But the great question concerns temporal reward: whether Christian charity, rightly performed, will be rewarded here in this life with temporal blessings. That is, is there ground to expect that what men give by way of charity will be returned here into their bosoms again with increase?

I do not deny that a charitable man may become poor and be brought into some straits. This may come through standing surety for others, through negligence in his calling, or because of some secret sin he lives in, which may justly bring a temporal curse on him. So in such cases his liberality may not be a sufficient fence against want and poverty. But this I say: as stinginess toward the poor is the readiest way to poverty, so Christian charity, rightly performed, is the surest way to plenty and abundance. It is usually rewarded with temporal blessings here, as well as with eternal blessings hereafter. Where is the man to be found who is the poorer for what he has given to the poor? How many are the instances of those who have met with some remarkable blessings from God in this life as the reward of their liberality!

To many uncharitable men this may seem a paradox, that giving should be the surest way of getting, and that the more generous any man is, the more likely he is to thrive and prosper in the world. Yet nothing is more clearly laid down in the Scripture, or found to be true by the experience of multitudes of God’s people in all ages. And I am truly persuaded that there is seldom any man who makes conscience of this duty, and gives out to the poor in proportion to what God has bestowed on him, and with an honest, upright heart, who will not find what he gave doubled and redoubled on him in temporal blessings, if he observes the dealings of God’s providence toward him. I dare challenge all the world to give one instance, or at least any considerable number of instances, of any truly merciful men whose charity has ruined them. But as living wells spring and flow the more freely the more they are drawn, so the wealth of charitable men often, if not ordinarily, multiplies in the very giving out of it, even as the five loaves and few fish multiplied in the breaking and distributing of them. And the widow’s oil increased by being poured out.

But these bare assertions are not full proof. So, to clear the truth of this doctrine better, I will prove it by Scriptures, examples and reasons.

Proofs from Scripture

1. For Scripture proofs, there are very many in both the Old and the New Testament. What the apostle says of godliness in 1 Tim 4:8, that it “is profitable for all things, holding promise for the present life and for the one to come,” I may say of charity: it is profitable for all things, holding promises of temporal blessings as well as of spiritual and eternal ones.

Deut 15:10: “Give generously to your brother, and do not let your heart be grieved when you do so. And because of this the Lord your God will bless you in all your work and in everything to which you put your hand.” It is not your own labor or care but the divine blessing that makes rich, and see, here is a Scripture deed that settles that blessing on the generous. We have the like in Prov 3:9, 10: “Honor the Lord with your wealth,” by giving out a portion of it for the relief of the poor, “then your barns will be filled with plenty.” And as your barns, so your shop, your cellars and warehouses, where you store your goods, will be filled with abundance: “and your vats will burst with new wine.” This seems to be a hyperbole, yet it means no less than this: that God’s usual way is to make good returns of all we lay out on him and his; and that our wisest way, both to secure and to increase what we have, is to make ourselves creditors to his needy saints.

A compassionate heart and a helping hand will gather by spending. Such giving is getting; such bounty is the shortest way to plenty. So the wise man adds, in Prov 11:24: “One scatters, yet increases all the more; another withholds more than is right, only to become poor.” Who is it here who scatters? Not the man who wastes his estate on his throat, his back and his belly, or, with the prodigal, on harlots; but the man who “casts his bread upon the waters,” as the expression is in Eccl 11:1; the man who “has scattered abroad his gifts to the poor,” as in Ps 112:9. This is the scatterer in that text. And what of him? Is he wasted? Is he impoverished? See, the very opposite: the man has grown rich; he is increased by scattering. Let the man who withholds more than is right look to it: he is the more likely of the two to be found shortly on the dunghill. If you would secure yourself from beggary, do not keep God’s beggars from your door. Do not send away empty those whose needs, though not their tongues, cry in your ears, Give for the Lord’s sake. Do not fear to lose by laying out. Your laying up what you should lay out has the most danger in it. The divine curse may wither in your hand what you hold fast against the divine command.

In the following verse we read further, “The generous soul will be made fat.” The soul is often taken in Scripture to mean the man, and so it is here: it is the same as the generous man. To be made fat means to prosper, to be full and abound, or to grow rich in this world’s goods. And so it will be, if this Scripture may be believed.

The generous soul: in the Hebrew, as you+ may find it noted in the margin, it is the soul of blessing. The merciful man is a blessing, and has a blessing for those who need him; and he who is a blessing will be blessed. The Lord God will bless him with an increase of his wealth, the man who has most emptied himself for God and his people. It is true that the soul of the generous man, taken in the proper sense, will be a gainer by his liberality. No Christians are more thriving than the merciful Christians; what they spend in temporal things is abundantly returned in spiritual things. But there is so much of the carnal even in too many Christians, and we need encouragements suited to our natures. So these outward encouragements are added to our spiritual advantages (which are the greatest), since they often take hold most on our too carnal hearts. So this is the sense of the place: the generous man, as the reward and encouragement of his liberality, will prosper in the world. And as it follows, he who waters the soul of the needy, his waters will not fail, but he will himself be watered also. God will give back to him according as he has given out to others.

And for their further encouragement the wise man says, in Prov 19:17: “Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the Lord, and He will repay him for what he has given.” If what you give is repaid to you again, how can it be said to be lost? Indeed the poor to whom you give are not able to repay you. Yet you have so all-sufficient a surety as God himself, who has undertaken the repayment, so you need not doubt of it. Oh, happy is the man who becomes a creditor to his Creator and makes God his debtor! The earth is God’s, and all its fullness. Heaven and earth will be emptied before such a man goes without a royal payment.

Do not fear to be a usurer, so long as you lend to God. Make him your debtor, and he will surely pay you principal and interest. Allow him his time (for that he will have), and he will not only pay the debt, but allow you something for your waiting. The ungodly man borrows and does not pay back; but this will never be said of the righteous God. He is just, and will make good payment of whatever is lent to him.

It is true that the Lord loves to deal on trust, and is accustomed to make payment by way of returns. He will be trusted; and those who will not give him credit, let them put their estates into surer hands, if they can. And he is accustomed to pay by way of returns: it may be neither in the same kind nor in the same country. Sometimes he does not pay in the same kind, bread for bread, or clothes for clothes, or money for money. Nor perhaps will he make his payment in this foreign land where you are a merchant adventurer. He may give you his bill of exchange to receive it in your own country, that better country which is your home and inheritance, which will be the reward of your works and of the labor of love which you show to his name. And if he does this, does he do you any wrong? Is it not best for you to receive your goods at your home? Is it any harm to you to receive silver for your brass, gold for your silver, rubies for your gold, a treasure in heaven for your treasure on earth? Do not fear that he will fall behind in paying you. Yet do not balk, even if you should be put to wait for payment in full till hereafter. And for the present you may depend on this, from Prov 28:27: “Whoever gives to the poor will not lack.” He will have in hand what is needful at least. He will not lack: and there may be more in this word than if he had said, I will pay you all at once. For all that you have, though you hold it ever so close, cannot secure you from ever coming to want. Great as your abundance is, you may come to want before you die. But what your abundance cannot do, this promise of God can do, and does, for you: it gives you security that you will never lack.

Again, Eccl 11:1: “Cast your bread upon the waters, for after many days you will find it again.” By bread is meant here all things necessary for the support of men’s lives. And by casting their bread upon the waters is meant their giving freely of what they have for the relief of the poor, whose watery eyes betray their great need. What you bestow on them may seem as clearly lost and thrown away as what is thrown down the river or cast into the sea, where there is no likelihood of receiving it again, because it is given to those who can in no way repay you. From this arose that Greek proverb, εἰς ὕδωρ σπείρεις, you sow upon the water, which is usually applied to those who bestow kindnesses where they are utterly lost.

Yet “after many days you will find it again.” Lavater, in locum [on this passage], says that here is implied a promise of long life to the charitable man: that God will lengthen out his days to a good old age. Though this proves true in many, yet I do not think it is intended here, or is the meaning of the words. Rather the meaning is this: though your reward does not appear at once, yet if you bestow your alms with a sincere heart, it will not be lost, but will certainly be returned into your bosom with increase.

The Lord says yet further by the prophet in Isa 58:7, 8, etc.: “If you share your bread with the hungry, and bring the poor and homeless into your home, and clothe the naked when you see him, and do not hide yourself from your own flesh and blood,” by turning your face from him, “then” (see what a gracious promise of remarkable blessings follows on this) “your light will break forth like the dawn.” That is, then the night of your adversity will be driven away, and the dawn of your prosperity will break forth like the morning light. “Your righteousness will go before you”: that is, the fruit and reward of your charity will be visible to all. “The glory of the Lord will be your rear guard”: that is, the God of glory will by his power and providence both go before you and follow you with his blessing. And verse 10: “If you draw out your soul to the hungry and satisfy the afflicted soul,” that is, give him such hearty relief as will satisfy his need, “then your light will go forth in the darkness”: your adversity will be turned into prosperity. And “the Lord will always guide you; He will satisfy your soul in drought”: as you satisfied the poor man’s soul by supplying his needs, so the Lord will supply you with enough in the greatest dearth and famine. “And He will strengthen your frame. You will be like a well-watered garden, like a spring whose waters never fail”: an emblem of a flourishing and prosperous condition, which usually follows and accompanies merciful men.

Yes, our blessed Savior in Matt 19:29 promises that those who for his sake part with their estates, in this or any other way, or with any part or portion of them, will receive a hundredfold here, and inherit eternal life hereafter. Here in this life a man will have the return of a hundredfold. Many Christians have found this true in their own experience, and with thankfulness to God have acknowledged as much.

And what a variety of expressions our Savior uses in Luke 6:38 to assure us of a large reward here for all our labor of love shown to his ministers and members! “Give,” he says, “and it will be given to you+ again: a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over.” For your+ encouragement to this duty of giving to the poor, our Savior first adds a general promise of return: “Give, and it will be given to you+ again.” In this he gives you+ a bill in his own hand that you+ will be no loser by what you+ give to his poor, but will be repaid, and that with advantage, as the following words declare: you+ will have “a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over.” We count it good measure when it is heaped up. When it is not only heaped up but pressed down, that is more. But when it is heaped up, pressed down, and then heaped up and running over again, who can help saying that this is good measure indeed? Yet this is how God deals with merciful men: they will have mercies and blessings heaped up, pressed down, and running over. How truly, then, may I take up the words of the psalmist: “Blessed is the one who cares for the poor”! He will not only be blessed, but he will have blessings heaped up and running over! The apostle St. Paul expresses this very emphatically by the comparison of reaping and sowing (2 Cor 9:6): “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.” As men sow, so will they reap: the more liberally they give to good uses, the more bountifully they will receive from God. They will find a plentiful harvest as the fruit of all their cost and pains. Dr. Hammond, in his Practical Catechism, quoting these words of the apostle, “whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully,” adds this gloss: “By reaping bountifully, I take it, is meant not only God’s abundant repayments of glory in another world, but even his payments of temporal plenty and blessings here to those who have been willing to make that Christian use of the earthly talent committed to their stewardship.”

So you+ see that there are so many promises, in both the Old and the New Testament, of temporal as well as of spiritual and eternal blessings to the merciful, that no question can be made of the truth of the doctrine. And to use the expression of the doctor mentioned before: “By all these testimonies from the word of God, in both the New and the Old Testament, I take this doctrine to be as clear as any in the Scripture: that the promise of temporal plenty to the generous is so distinct and infallible that it can be no less than

  1. a very gross ignorance of plain Scripture not to observe it, and
  2. an act of downright unbelief not to believe it.”

The Testimonies of Divines

These proofs from Scripture are enough to convince any Christian of the truth of the doctrine. Yet for your+ further satisfaction I will briefly give you+ the judgment of some ancient fathers, and of some modern divines, on the same.

Non qui habet et Servat, sed qui impertit est Dives, et impertitio, non autem possessio divites facit. Clemens Alexand. Paedag. Lib. 3. Not he who possesses wealth and keeps it by him, but he who distributes it, is rich; nor is it the having but the laying out of riches that makes men rich.

Terrena omnia Servando amittimus, largiendo Servamus. Isiodorus. We lose all earthly things by keeping them, and by giving them away we keep them.

Lucrum est egenis dare, says St. Basil. It is the best way of thriving to give to those who are in want.

Faecundus est ager pauperum, cito reddit donantibus fructum. Aug. Serm. De Divite. The field of the poor is very fruitful, and quickly yields an increase to the charitable.

The same Father, in his 25th sermon de verbis Domini [on the words of the Lord], brings in Christ speaking like this: Da mihi ex eo quod dedi tibi, habuisti me largitorem, fac me debitorem, etc. Give to me of what I have given to you. I have been your benefactor; make me your debtor. Become a usurer to me, and I will pay you with advantage. And in one of his epistles: Da modicum ut recipias centuplum. Give a little, and you will receive a hundredfold.

Da pauperi ut detur tibi, quicquid pauperi dederis tu habebis, quod non dederis, habebit alter. Give to the poor, and it will be given to you. Whatever you give to the poor, you secure to yourself; what you withhold, another will possess. Pet. Raven Serm. Quodam.

Deus bis solvit hoc faenus, scilicet semel in terra, Secundo in caelo. In terra enim eleemosynariis multiplicat opes, in caelo autem longe plura, et majora rependit. God pays twice what is lent to him: once in this world, by multiplying the wealth of almsgivers, and then in heaven, where he pays it over and over. Cornelius a lapid. In Prov 19:17.

Dr. Hammond, in his sermon on Deut 26:12, 13, lays down this proposition: that almsgiving or mercifulness was never the wasting or lessening of any man’s estate, to himself or his posterity, but rather the increasing of it. And on this he adds: If I have delivered a new doctrine, which will not at once be believed, such as not every hearer will agree to, I do not doubt that there are plain texts of Scripture, more than one, which will assure every Christian of the truth of it. Consider them at your+ leisure: Ps 41:1, 2; Ps 112, all to this purpose; Prov 11:25; 22:9; 19:17; 28:27. Add to these the words of Christ in Mark 10:30. Though they are spoken more generally of any kind of parting with possessions for Christ’s sake, St. Jerome applies them to the words of Solomon in Prov 11:24, “One scatters, yet increases all the more,” quia centuplum accipiunt in hoc tempore, because, he says, they receive a hundredfold in this world.

All these put together, he says, must (to my understanding) make it as clear to any who acknowledge them as Scripture as if God should call to a man out of heaven by name, and bid him “relieve that poor man, and you will never be the poorer for it,” etc.

Afterward, in pressing the duty of almsgiving on his hearers, he says: This I am fully persuaded of: it is lack of belief, and nothing else, that keeps men from the practice of this duty. If this one mountain could be removed, the lessening of our wealth, of which almsgiving is accused; if that one stumbling block to flesh and blood could be kicked out of the way, there is no other devil that would take the unmerciful man’s part, and no other temptation that would trouble the almsgiver.

And let me tell you+ this: you+ have no more evidence for the truth of Christ’s coming, for all the fundamentals of your+ faith, on which you+ are content that your+ salvation should depend, than such evidence as I have given you+ for your+ assurance on this point.

Dr. Jeremy Taylor, in his Rules of Holy Living, treating of alms (Sect. 8), has this among other motives to it: That portion of our estate out of which a tenth, or a fifth, or a twentieth, or some offering to God for religion and the poor goes forth, certainly returns with a great blessing on all the rest. It is like the pouring out of oil by the Sidonian woman: as long as she poured into empty vessels, it could never stop running. Or it is like the widow’s barrel of meal: it was not used up as long as she fed the prophet.

Mr. Hildersham, in his 22nd lecture on Ps 51, speaking of almsgiving, says: “It is a duty to which God has made greater promises than to almost any other that a Christian can perform.” And there are three sorts of promises made to it. First, “that it will never hinder or beggar a man; that what is given in this way will not be lost.” Yes, it will return again with advantage and increase; yes, what is given in this way will bring God’s blessing on all that we have besides (Deut 15:10).

Dr. Thomas Jacomb, in his sermon on Matt 5:7, preached at the Spital in 1657, says: God will return to the merciful man what he gives to the poor. He will reward him in kind: whatever it is that he bestows, it will be made up to him again in the very kind. Many have found this to be true. In the morning they have given, it may be, five shillings, and before night God has unexpectedly brought them in twenty for it. The best way for a man to increase his estate is charity: money here is like the widow’s oil; the more it is poured out, the more it increases, etc. And on p. 26: No man will be the poorer at the year’s end for what he lays out on the poor; you+ will have your+ money again, and a profit on it too.

The author of The Whole Duty of Man, treating of alms in Partition 17, says there is only one objection to be made against a cheerful giving of alms, and that is the danger of impoverishing oneself by what one gives. To this he answers in these words: This is surely a vain supposition, since God has particularly promised the contrary to the charitable, that it will bring blessings on them, even in these outward things. “The generous soul will be made fat, and he who waters will himself be watered also” (Prov 11:25). “Whoever gives to the poor will not lack” (Prov 28:27). And there are many such texts, so that one may truly say this objection is grounded in direct unbelief. The short of it is, we dare not trust God. For this giving to the poor is directly putting our wealth into his hands: “Whoever gives to the poor lends to the Lord” (Prov 19:17). And that, too, on a solemn promise of repayment, as it follows in that verse: “and He will repay him for what he has given.” Among men it is thought a great slight when we refuse to trust them: it shows that we think them either not able to pay or not honest. What a vile affront to God it is, then, to distrust him like this! Indeed, what horrid blasphemy, to doubt the security of what he has so expressly passed his word for, he who is the Lord of all, and therefore cannot be insufficient, and who is the God of truth, and therefore will not fail to make good his promise! So do not let that unbelieving fear of future want shrink and shut up your heart against your poor brother. For though he is never likely to pay, yet God becomes his surety and enters into bond with him, and will most assuredly pay you with increase.

So it is so far from being a loss to you to give in this way that it is your great advantage. Any man would rather put his money in some sure hand, where he may both make it grow and be certain of having it when he needs it, than let it lie unprofitable by him, especially if he is in danger of thieves or other accidents by which he may well lose it. Now, alas, all that we possess is in imminent danger of being lost. There are countless accidents which may in an instant bring a rich man to beggary. Let him who doubts this only read the story of Job, and he will find an example of it there. So what course could be more prudent for our wealth than to put it out of the reach of those accidents by lending it to God in this way, where we may be sure to find it ready at our greatest need, and that with profit and increase too? It is in this respect that the apostle compares alms to seed (2 Cor 9:10). We know it is the nature of seed that is sown to multiply and increase; and so do all our acts of mercy. They do not return to us single and bare, but bring their sheaves in with them, a most plentiful and bountiful harvest. God does not deal with our alms as we too often deal with his graces, wrapping them up in a napkin so that they never bring in any advantage to us. No, he makes us most rich returns. So we have every reason to set about this duty most cheerfully, yes, joyfully, since we have such invitations to it, as much in respect of our own interest as of our neighbors’ needs.

So you+ have the truth of the point proved by both divine and human testimonies. I should now go on to give you+ some instances to confirm it further. But first I must beg you+ to take these two cautions.

1. Do not ascribe the reward to any merit of your+ good works, but only to the free grace and rich mercy of God. It is his rich mercy that we have the means to give, his free grace that we have a heart to give, and his abundant goodness that he accepts our works of charity and rewards them with all sorts of blessings, temporal, spiritual and eternal. But we cannot merit anything at his hand by giving him what is his own.

2. Our alms-deeds are sacrifices acceptable and well-pleasing to God through Christ, and he has bound himself by many gracious promises to reward them both here and hereafter. Yet far be it from us to perform them merely out of hope of reward. Let us rather perform them for conscience’ sake, in obedience to the command of God (who has required them at our hands), and in testimony of our thankfulness to him for what he has graciously bestowed on us. We are commanded to obey the magistrate not so much for fear of punishment and hope of reward as for conscience’ sake, in obedience to the command of God (Rom 13:5). So we ought to give our alms not so much for the sake of the reward as out of conscience, for the Lord’s sake.

I do not deny that Christians in their well-doing may, for their encouragement, have regard to the recompense of reward, but not only or chiefly. The chief and principal ends we should aim at in all our good works are the glory of God and obedience to his command. Our regard for the recompense of reward ought to be subordinate to these. The truth is, this temporal reward should be looked on not so much as an argument to persuade us to give, but as an answer to an objection against giving. You will be ready to say, I may need it myself, or those who are mine may need it. But only believe that God will repay you, and with more besides, and then that doubt will be taken out of the way.

Examples out of Scripture and History

With these two cautions set down first, I will go on to confirm the point from the examples of many charitable persons who have been abundantly rewarded in temporal mercies for the kindness they have shown to the ministers and members of Christ.

The widow of Zarephath fed the prophet Elijah in her house during the whole time of famine. And how abundantly the Lord rewarded this charity of hers! He miraculously preserved and increased her flour and oil, by which her family was fed. He also restored her son to life again after his soul had departed (1 Kgs 17:22). And he caused the prophet to stay with her many months, to feed her soul with spiritual food, as she had fed his body with bodily food.

How abundantly the Shunammite’s kindness to the prophet Elisha was rewarded!

  1. By the gift of a son after long barrenness.
  2. By restoring her son to life again when he was dead (2 Kgs 4:35).
  3. By warning her beforehand of a famine that was coming (2 Kgs 8:1, 4).
  4. By the restoring of her house and land, lost in her long absence because of the famine (2 Kgs 8:6).

Notable is the instance of Job. What a merciful man he was, we may read in Job 29:12, 13, 15: “I rescued the poor who cried out and the fatherless who had no helper. The dying man blessed me, and I made the widow’s heart sing for joy. … I served as eyes to the blind and as feet to the lame. I was a father to the needy.” And in Job 31:16, 22: “If I have denied the desires of the poor or allowed the widow’s eyes to fail, if I have eaten my morsel alone, not sharing it with the fatherless, … if I have seen one perish for lack of clothing, or a needy man without a cloak, if his heart has not blessed me for warming him with the fleece of my sheep, … then may my arm fall from my shoulder and be torn from its socket.” I have copied out his own words at this length so that I might set this worthy pattern before the reader’s eyes.

But you+ will say: What became of this merciful man? Did he prosper? Did he flourish and grow great? Who was so poor as poor Job, after all these acts of mercy? How long was it afterward before we find this merciful man a miserable man, stripped bare of all that he ever had? But, first, it was not his own mercy but Satan’s malice that brought him down. It was the devil who set the Sabeans and Chaldeans on him, to plunder and carry away all that he had. And secondly, what became of Job afterward, after Satan had done his worst? You+ may read in ch. 42:10, etc., that “the Lord restored” Job’s “prosperity and doubled his former possessions”; that He “blessed Job’s latter days more than his first. He owned fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, a thousand yoke of oxen, and a thousand female donkeys”; and that he “also had seven sons and three daughters.”

Acts 28:7: we read how Publius, the chief man of the island of Malta (where St. Paul and many others with him were cast by shipwreck), received them and lodged them courteously for three days. And in the next verse we read how the father of Publius, when he lay desperately sick of a fever and dysentery, was healed by St. Paul and restored to his former health. So likewise the kindness which the islanders showed to Paul and his fellow travelers was rewarded with the cure of many of their sick.

To these examples recorded in Scripture I will add a few more out of ancient and modern writings.

St. Alban (whom Mr. Foxe, in his first volume, mentions among the martyrs who suffered for the name and cause of Christ) received a poor persecuted minister into his house. He was so worked on by the minister’s godly life and gracious exhortations that he turned from heathenism to Christianity, and at last suffered as a martyr for the truth of Jesus Christ, as Bede and others write of him. His kindness to a poor persecuted minister was rewarded not only with his conversion to the true religion, but also with the honor of martyrdom.

St. Augustine, having set forth the mercifulness and liberality of Constantine the Great, says, Bonus Deus, Constantinum Magnum tantis terrenis implevit muneribus, etc. God gave Constantine, that merciful prince, more wealth than heart could wish, for his bounty to the poor. Aug. De Civitate. Dei. L. 5.

Dr. Hammond, in the treatise mentioned before, tells an ancient story out of Cedrenus of a Jew. On reading those words of Solomon in Prov 19:17, “Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the Lord, and He will repay him for what he has given,” this Jew resolved to test whether God would be as good as his word. So he gave all that he had to the poor except two pieces of silver, and then waited, expecting to see it come back again. But when that expectation was not answered at once, he grew angry, and went up to Jerusalem to remonstrate with God for not keeping his promise. Going on his way, he found two men striving together, locked in a quarrel that could not be settled, about a stone which they had both found on the road as they walked together. So both had an equal right to it; but since it was only one stone and could not be divided, they could not both have it. And so, to make them friends, he took his two pieces of silver and by agreement divided them between the two men, and had the stone in exchange for them. With the stone he went on his journey, and coming to Jerusalem, he showed it to the goldsmith. The goldsmith told him that it was a jewel of great value, a stone that had fallen and been lost out of the high priest’s ephod; if he took it to the high priest, he would certainly receive a great reward. He did so, and so it proved. The high priest took it from him, gave him a great reward, and at the same time sharply rebuked him for questioning the truth of God’s promises, bidding him trust God the next time.

The story of Tiberius the Second is to the purpose here. Take it in the words of that reverend person mentioned before, in his sermon at the Spital. This Tiberius was very famous for his bounty to the poor, so much so that his wife used to blame him for it. Once, when she spoke to him of how he wasted his treasure in this way, he told her that he would never lack money, so long as he supplied the needs of the poor in obedience to Christ’s command. And see how quickly providence ordered it! Immediately after he had given much in this way, he found a great treasure under a marble table which was taken up. And news was brought him too of the death of one Narses, a very rich man, who had left his whole estate to him.

Famous is the story of that charitable bishop of Milan. As he was traveling with his servant, he overtook some poor people who begged an alms of him. So he asked his man what money he had about him. The servant answered, Three crowns, and the bishop commanded him to give them to the poor people. But the servant, thinking himself wiser than his master, gave them only two crowns, not knowing what need they might have for money before they got home. Not long after, some noblemen met the bishop, and knowing him to be a very charitable man, ordered two hundred crowns to be paid to the bishop’s servant for his master’s use. When the servant had received the money, he at once told his master of it with great joy. On this the bishop said: Now you may see how, in wronging the poor of their due by keeping back the third crown which I intended for them, you have wronged me as well. Si enim tres dedisses, trecentos accepisses, etc. If you had given those three crowns I commanded you to give, you would have received three hundred crowns, whereas now I have only two hundred. Melanc. Apud Joh. Manlium in Loc. Com.

It is recorded of Mary, the wife of Alexander Farnese, Prince of Parma, that being childless, she came to hope that if she would take into her house some orphan, or poor man’s child, and bring him up there, God would give her a son. So she took a poor man’s son into her care and gave orders for his education. And as she had hoped, at the end of nine months she gave birth to a son.

Fitting to this point also is the story of one John Stewart, provost of Ayr in Scotland, who was eminent for piety and charity. He had a considerable estate left him by his father, a great part of which he gave to the poor and to other charitable uses. To pass by many instances, I will mention only one. At one time his heart was much moved by the poverty and needs of many of God’s people who were in a suffering condition. So he sent for several of them to come to Edinburgh. When they had met there, and some time had been spent in prayer, he made them promise not to reveal what he was about to do as long as he lived. Then he told them that he was not unaware how low a condition many of them were in, and so he had brought some money with him to lend to each of them, but on these terms: that they should never offer to repay it until he asked for it. Soon after this, such a plague broke out in Ayr, the place where he lived, that trade greatly decayed, and he himself, with others, was brought into straits. On this some of the profane in that place mocked him, saying that religion had made him poor, and that his giving so much to others, like a fool, had brought him to want. But mark what followed. Having borrowed a little money, he went from Ayr to Rochelle in France. There salt and other goods were exceedingly cheap for lack of trade, and he ventured to freight a ship, and loaded her on credit. Then he went back again through England to Ayr in Scotland, having ordered the ship to come there. But after long waiting he was told for certain that his ship had been taken by a Turkish man-of-war. The report of this afflicted him exceedingly. It was not that he did not know how to be brought low as well as how to abound, but he feared that the mouths of wicked men would be opened all the more to reproach his profession of faith and his charity. But soon after, news was brought him that his ship had arrived safely in the roadstead, and when he went out he saw that it was true. And through God’s good providence, as a reward of his charity, he made so much from the goods in the ship that after paying his debts he had twenty thousand marks left for himself. Though his bread was cast upon the waters, and to all appearance lost, yet after many days it returned to him with great advantage. I read this story lately in a book called The Fulfilling of the Scriptures.

Examples of Our Own Time

Daniel Waldow Esquire, citizen and Mercer, who was chosen alderman of London, is a further proof of the doctrine laid down before. From my own experience I could say much of his bounty and charity, and also of the plentiful estate with which God blessed him for it. But I will rather give it to you+ in the words of that holy man and blessed servant of Christ in the work of the ministry, Mr. James Nalton, now with God. He was more closely acquainted with Mr. Waldow, and so all the more fit to preach his funeral sermon and to set out his life for our imitation. His words are these: “He was a man eminent and exemplary in the grace of charity, as appeared by his great bounty shown on every occasion. No good man, minister or other, who came to propose any work of charity, public or private, ever needed to do more than propose it. For his heart was so set on works of mercy that he forestalled any pressing request by his Christian and heroic liberality. He made no more of giving ten pounds to a work of charity than many other rich men make of giving ten shillings. His charity had two rare things that went with it, which made it all the more remarkable and worthy of praise.

1. “He did good while he lived. He carried his lantern before him: he made his own hands his executors and his own eyes his overseers. Some will part with their riches when they can keep them no longer. This is like a cutpurse who, when he is spotted or chased, will drop a purse of gold because he can keep it no longer. But to be doing good in our lifetime, while we have opportunity, is an act of faith, and an evidence that we can trust God with our estate and our children, that he will provide for them when our heads are laid in the grave.

2. “He gave out his charity so secretly, without any self-seeking or pharisaical vainglory, that his left hand did not know what his right hand was doing. So he would often go with a hundred pounds under his cloak to some godly friends, asking them to distribute it among such honest poor people as stood in most need of relief.”

In short, he did so much good while he lived, as if he meant to have nothing to do when he died; and yet he gave so generously when he came to die, as if he had done no good while he lived.

Many, I know, are apt to say that they have many children, and so cannot give. So had Mr. Waldow: he had nine children alive at his death. But providing for them was no hindrance to his charity, and his charity did no harm to his children; rather, it secured a blessing on them.

Mr. John Walter, citizen and Draper of London, was remarkably charitable, not only at his death but in the whole course of his life, even from his younger years. To avoid vainglory, his way was to send considerable sums of money to various poor families by the hands of others, whose faithfulness he could rely on. For this, God not only blessed him with a large estate, but also gave him such contentment in it that he sat down abundantly satisfied. And he made a solemn vow and promise to God that he would give the surplus of his estate, whatever might come to him in the future from his calling and business, to charitable uses. That you+ may be assured of the truth of this, I have given you+ here his own words, copied out of his last will and testament, which are as follows.

I thought fit to declare that about twenty years ago, when the Lord had entrusted me with a suitable estate, sufficient to maintain those in my charge and to provide fit portions for my wife and children after my death, I resolved that whatever further estate the Lord should be pleased to entrust me with, I would bestow it on charitable uses.

After this vow, finding his estate wonderfully increased, he began to build almshouses: one in the parish of St. George in Southwark, another in St. Mary Newington. For in those parishes, he observed, there were many blind, lame and distressed poor people, and not one almshouse in them. He also built a chapel near one of his almshouses, for the poor people to serve God in daily. Having built his almshouses, he bought lands and houses of inheritance with the poor’s stock, and settled them on the Drapers’ Company, both for the relief and support of his almspeople after his death, and for carrying out the other charitable gifts named in his last will and testament. While he lived, he used to go himself once a month to his almshouses in his worst clothes (so that he might not be suspected of being their founder), and gave the poor people their promised allowance. No doubt the best charity is that which, like the Nile, has its various streams seen, but its fountain hidden. Having built his almshouses and endowed them with a good income, he then relieved poor people and families with considerable sums of money out of the rest of his poor’s stock (which increased daily through God’s blessing on his work and efforts in his calling). And he gave much bread every week to the poor of several outer parishes. All this he did while he was still living, besides what he gave on the same account at his death, which was also very considerable, as his will further shows. And in spite of all this, he gave and left about ten thousand pounds to his wife and his two daughters. This, without question, is the surest way to have our WILLS carried out: to see them carried out in our own lifetime, since many executors prove executioners of WILLS.

William Pennoyer Esquire, citizen and merchant of London, was a person made wholly of mercy and goodness, bounty and liberality, which he showed in the whole course of his life, from the time he first set up in the world. Many years before his death, he turned a great part of the stock he traded with into lands of inheritance, to the value of four hundred pounds a year. Being eminently charitable, he lived as frugally as he could, spending about two hundred pounds a year on himself, his wife and his family; and the rest of his income he gave wholly to charitable uses. So I have been told by those who lived long with him and were closely related to him.

To give you+ a clear demonstration of his Christian charity, and of God’s repaying it to him here in this life with temporal blessings, I will list some of the legacies he left to charitable uses in his last will and testament, passing over those he gave to his rich relatives and friends.

To poor ministers, widows, and others in distress, about £150

To four of his poor tenants, £20

Also £800, to be laid out here in woolen cloth or other goods, to be sent to New England for the use of his poor relatives there.

He gave lands to the value of twenty pounds a year to certain trustees, to pay for the schooling of forty boys.

To Bristol, £54 a year toward the maintenance of a schoolmaster and lecturer to preach a weekday lecture there; and to other charitable uses.

He also settled £20 a year on trustees for the schooling of forty poor children in or near Whitechapel, and 40 shillings a year to buy Bibles for some of the children.

He gave £12 a year for the maintaining of a school at the Hay in Brecknockshire, and 40 shillings more a year to buy books for the scholars.

Also £10 a year for the maintenance of poor distressed people in the Hospital of Bethlehem in London.

And £10 a year to ten of the blindest, oldest and poorest clothworkers, at the discretion of the masters, wardens and assistants of that company for the time being.

He gave £40 a year to Christ-church Hospital, for apprenticing four children a year, and 40 shillings more a year to buy each of the children a Bible.

Besides these, he gave his poor relatives more than two thousand pounds by his will.

And by a codicil attached to it, he left to certain trustees a thousand pounds to be given to honest poor people, and also £300 for releasing poor prisoners. These sums have been paid into the hands of the trustees by Mr. Richard Loton and Michael Davison Esq., who to their honor proved themselves faithful executors of this charitable will.

Thomas Arnold, citizen and Haberdasher of London: when he first set up for himself, his stock was not great. But being charitably disposed and ready for every good work, he saw his estate, through God’s blessing, increase very much.

His charity in his lifetime appeared not only in his eagerness to share with those he saw in want, for their relief, but also in his frequent inquiries of others after poor people who were overburdened with children or otherwise distressed. Indeed, he paid men to make it their business to find honest poor people on whom he might bestow his charity. He also entrusted others with considerable sums of money to distribute among the poorest, charging them to have special regard to the honest poor, those whom they judged truly feared God. That he was no loser but a gainer by his liberality is plain from this: God so blessed him in his calling that he attained to an alderman’s estate, and was chosen to that office. More than that, he gave up his calling in the city and withdrew to the country, so that he might better mind God and the concerns of his soul more, and the world and its concerns less.

John Clark, doctor of medicine, was a man of great repute for his learning, piety and charity, and for a while President of the College of Physicians. His custom was to lay aside all his Lord’s Day fees as a sacred stock for charitable uses. What he received on God’s day he devoted entirely to God, counting it a kind of sacrilege to take it for himself or for any common use. For this the Lord was pleased so to prosper him in his calling that, though at first his practice was small and his estate not very great, afterward his practice so increased, and the world so flowed in on him, that he lived plentifully and comfortably, and gave his children generous portions.

The same was also practiced by John Bathurst, doctor of medicine, whom I knew very well. His Lord’s Day fees were always kept as a bank for the poor, wholly devoted to their use and spent on it. This was so far from lessening his income that, by the blessing of God on his practice, it was greatly increased by it in a few years. For when he first came to London, he brought little estate with him and had few acquaintances here, Yorkshire being his native county, where he had spent his former days. Yet the Lord was pleased so to prosper him in his calling that in twenty years he bought lands of inheritance to the value of a thousand pounds a year. I say what I know to be certain; for in the opinion of some, his estate at his death was worth no less than two thousand pounds a year.

Dr. Edmond Trench also followed the same course, as his wife and various other friends of his testify. And it is certain that this was no damage but a great advantage to him; for he had as many patients as his weak body would allow him to visit. And though he lived in a full and plentiful way, often and cheerfully entertaining ministers and scholars at his table, yet he gained a very considerable estate, which he left to his wife and children; and in them not only his memory but his piety still lives on.

I have good grounds to believe that many other physicians make conscience of this duty. But oh, that all would do the same! They would certainly be no losers by it at the year’s end, but would find God’s blessing on their calling and estates, prospering them in both.

And here a case of conscience comes to my mind that is worth inquiring into, namely, whether physicians may lawfully take their Lord’s Day fees for their own private use. I mean the fees they receive from their patients on the Sabbath day.

I do not deny that works of mercy may and ought to be done on that day. For the Lord says, “I desire mercy, not sacrifice” (Matt 9:13), that is, mercy rather than sacrifice. Nor do I deny that physicians may receive their fees for their pains, from the richer sort especially. But I very much question whether they may take those fees for themselves. For the Lord has given us six days out of seven, in which we may and ought to follow our callings for our own livelihood and that of those who belong to us; but he has sanctified and set apart the Christian Sabbath for his own honor and service. So it seems only reasonable that what comes to us on that day should be set apart and used for his more immediate use and service. But I will not impose this as a necessary duty, at least not on all, since circumstances may differ. For now I leave it to be settled by the consciences of those who are most concerned in it.

Samuel Dunche of Pusey, in the County of Berks, Esquire, was a person who, according to the apostle’s rule, did good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith. His custom was to send money every year to several towns for the relief of their poor, such as Stow upon the Woolds [Stow-on-the-Wold] in Gloucestershire, Norliche [Northleach], Lamburn [Lambourn], and others not mentioned here. And on the last named he settled lands of inheritance forever for the same use. And to Rumsey [Romsey] in Hampshire he gave by deed, on the same account, a lease of 99 years, to begin after his death. The poor of that town also, whom he called his almspeople, had weekly relief from him during his life, and many other towns along with them had a large share in the same bounty.

He sent several poor children of that town to school, and also some of those belonging to Faringdon, and he not only paid for their schooling but also supplied them with all such books as were fit and suitable for them. He also had several good books printed at his own expense, which he gave freely to the poor, so that they might be the more encouraged to read and to acquaint themselves with the concerns of another and better life.

He further gave considerable sums of money every year for the constant supply of such godly ministers as he knew to be in want. And on several of them he settled considerable annuities, £10 and £20 a year for their lives, besides the legacies, not small ones, that he gave to some of them at his death.

Besides all this, his hand was always open and ready to give whenever any fit occasion was offered him. Indeed, such was the largeness of his heart and the tenderness of his compassion that he could hardly pass by anyone he judged a proper object of his charity without contributing freely and bountifully to that person’s relief.

So this pious gentleman honored God with his wealth, and ventured on the words of the royal prophet, to cast his bread upon the waters. The unbelieving world counts this mere folly and usually reckons it among its losses. Yet he, to his advantage, according to the promise attached to it, found it again, and not after many days. This bread, like the loaves with which Christ fed the multitude, was multiplied in his hands, and his oil increased by pouring out. He was only a younger brother, and the estate settled on him was only £800 a year, or thereabouts. And yet, in spite of this (I had almost said) excess of charity, his estate was so far from being ruined, or in the least diminished, that not only the same bare measure he had received, but a much greater one, pressed down and running over, was measured out to him and his descendants. So remarkably did God reward his charity in this life, wisely ordering by his good providence that, one way or another, large handfuls were thrown into his bushel from various hands, as overmeasure. There is now left to his heirs an estate of more than double the value of what he received from his father, besides the portions he gave to all his daughters, five in number, which were very considerable, to some of them more than £2,000.

And here I hope I may, without offense or vainglory, take the liberty to mention, among others, the charity and liberality of my dear and honored father, Dr. William Gouge, late pastor of Blackfriars, London. He was eminent in other graces, and so also in that of charity. It was from him that I first heard that the tenth part of a rich man’s estate is a fit proportion to be devoted and dedicated to God for charitable uses. But though he commended that to others, yet by what I find in some papers written in his own hand, I may truly say that he gave the seventh part of all his yearly income toward maintaining poor scholars at the university and relieving poor families and distressed persons. And how wonderfully God blessed both his ministry and his outward estate is so well known to all who lived in his days that I suppose it needless for me to say anything about it. Only I may truly apply to him the words of the psalmist: “He is ever generous and quick to lend, and his children are blessed.”

Many more instances of the same kind might be added here. Some are of persons who are now with joy reaping in the other world the blessed fruit of the seed they sowed so plentifully in this one. Others are of persons still living among us, some of whom have acknowledged to me that God has already rewarded them a hundredfold for what they have lent to him by giving it to his poor. But those already mentioned may be abundantly sufficient to show the truth in hand, and to encourage and stir us up, in imitation of those worthies, to a more ready and conscientious practice of this great duty. It is so essential to Christianity, so well pleasing to God, so creditable to our profession of faith, and so beneficial, not only for our eternal happiness but for our present gain, comfort and prosperity here on earth.

The Reasons

The point being proved in this way by Scriptures and examples, we come now to the reasons, for its further confirmation.

1. Reason. It may be taken from the goodness and bounty of God, which is such that he will not allow any work of charity shown to any of his ministers or children to pass away unrewarded, without a full recompense. So David says in Ps 62:12, “To You, O Lord, belongs mercy. For You render to each man according to his work.” Though God does not render a reward to any man for his work done, yet he does render to every man according to his work. Indeed, God always rewards beyond measure, to give evidence of his grace and bounty. God will not be in any man’s debt for long; what a man has paid out on God’s account, he will speedily return into his bosom with advantage.

2. Reason. It may be taken from the faithfulness and righteousness of God. He has graciously promised in his word to recompense and reward our kindness abundantly, and his faithfulness and righteousness bind him to make good what he has promised, so that he cannot help but be as good as his word. Men may be quick to promise but slow to perform. But with God, who is the true and faithful one, dictum et factum, saying and doing, are one and the same: all his promises are Yes and Amen in Christ Jesus. The apostle says in Heb 6:10, “God is not unrighteous. He will not forget your+ work and labor of love which you+ have shown for His name as you+ have ministered to the saints and continue to do so.” Here the apostle argues that a reward is certain for those who minister anything to the saints, from the righteousness of God: because he is righteous, he will not fail to do what he has promised. He is not unrighteous so as to FORGET; that is, he will righteously remember. And God’s remembering means the same as his recompensing. As he will remember sinners by repaying their evil ways on their own heads, so he will remember his saints by returning the good they have done into their own bosoms.

To assure us all the more of this kind of remembrance from God, the Holy Spirit mentions certain books, or scrolls of remembrance written before God, in which the merciful deeds of his servants are recorded. So it is no more possible that those who are charitably kind and helpful to the poor ministers and people of God should lose their reward, than that God himself should cease to be righteous, or forget his word.

3. Reason. It may be taken from several metaphorical expressions used in Scripture, by which almsgiving is represented to us, all of which imply not only a certain return but a return with increase, such as SOWING, and LENDING, and that at usury.

(1.) We find it set out in Scripture by SOWING, 2 Cor 9:6: “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.” The apostle applies this proverbial saying to the giving out of alms. Now farmers who sow their grain with a liberal hand usually reap a crop to match. In the same way, Christians who sow their seed of charity with an open, plentiful hand will reap a plentiful crop to match. They will find that the seed they have sown comes up with increase, yielding thirty, if not sixty, or a hundredfold here, besides eternal life hereafter. It may be that you will not reap the fruit of your seed at once; and what wonder is that? Who is there that sows and expects to reap the same day? The farmer waits for his harvest. Wait on the Lord, and do not doubt that a harvest will come that will pay you both for your sowing and for your waiting.

(2.) The second metaphor by which almsgiving is set out in Scripture is LENDING, and lending at interest. Prov 19:17: “Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the Lord, and He will repay him for what he has given.” Men who lend to men receive their own back with increase. What they lay up lies dead, and the thief may perhaps break in and steal it; but what they lend, if it is to safe hands, comes back with advantage. How rich some usurers grow by this trade of lending! And though it is a paradox that giving is a richer trade than lending, even at interest, yet it is a certain truth. For this giving is lending, and the man who lends to the Lord will find a greater income at the year’s end than the man who lends to the best of men. So, as one well says, Eleemosyna non est divitiarum dispendium, sed ditescendi potius compendium, quaestusque; omnium uberrimus: giving to the poor is not the way to waste our wealth, but the art of thriving, and the shortest road to riches. Though our alms-deeds seem (like the seed sown) to perish and rot, yet if we believe what we do not see, we will surely see what we believe. We will find, even here, such a fruitful increase that we will conclude that giving to charitable uses is the surest and safest way of getting and thriving in the world.

So you+ have the truth of the point confirmed by Scriptures, examples, and reasons. We come now to the application.

A Use of Reproof

1. A use of reproof of all unmerciful men. God has laid many charges on us to be rich in good works, ready to give, willing to share, to draw out our souls to the hungry, to open our hearts to the needy, and he has given us many encouragements to this in his word; and yet these men shut up their hearts of compassion against the poor, refusing to give them any help or relief. Surely such men have no love for Christ. For who can say that he loves the Lord Jesus Christ in truth and sincerity, when he allows his ministers and members to go without necessities, even food and clothing? Is this your love for Christ, to let him starve? It is plain that you love your money more than Christ, and so you come under that fearful anathema in 1 Cor 16:22: “If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be Anathema Maranatha.” These two words, though both denote a curse, are from two different languages. The first word, Anathema, is a Greek word meaning accursed, and it is used so in Rom 9:3 and Gal 1:8. The second is a Syriac word, as Beza observes in his annotations on 1 Cor 16:22, yet often used by the Jews. It means our Lord comes: Maran is “our Lord,” and atha is “comes.” It implies that those who were under this curse were to expect no mercy, but to look for the dreadful coming of Christ to take vengeance on them. So, as St. James says in ch. 2:13, “Judgment without mercy will be shown to anyone who has not been merciful.” How do they think to find mercy from Christ, they who never showed mercy to him and his?

I will not condemn all for unmercifulness (God forbid that I should). There are many (and I wish to God there were more) who contribute bountifully to the needs both of ministers and of other poor saints of God. But I still have too much cause to say that the greatest part of the rich men among us have their hearts hardened and their compassion shut up, so that they cannot feel for the needs of the poor; and their hands are withered, like the hand of the man in the Gospel, so that they cannot stretch them out to any good use.

Oh, that such men would consider that unmercifulness is a greater sin than they imagine! It was one of Sodom’s sins, which brought down fire and brimstone from heaven on them and all their children (Ezek 16:49). Uncharitable men are cursed in their life, and so at their death; but they will be most cursed at the day of judgment. Being barren, fruitless trees in God’s orchard, they will surely be cut down with the barren fig tree and thrown into unquenchable fire.

To show you+ more particularly the miseries of uncharitable persons:

(1.) They are accursed here in everything: all they have is cursed. So much is implied in that saying of our Savior, Luke 11:41: “Give as alms such things as you+ have, and everything is clean for you+.” But without almsgiving nothing is clean for you+; that is, nothing is blessed and sanctified to you+, but all things are defiled and cursed. Not only are your+ crosses curses, but your+ blessings are curses to you+. So God threatens to curse their very blessings (Mal 2:2). Though you enjoy an abundance of this world’s goods, yet as long as you are hardhearted to the poor and needy, the curse of God clings to your store and abundance. Oh, how sad and lamentable your condition must be, when those things that are not only blessings in themselves, but blessed to others as well, are cursed to you! Surely, to be accursed like this is misery enough.

(2.) As the unmerciful are cursed here, so they will be cursed hereafter.
