Jas 2:13: “Judgment without mercy will be shown to anyone who has not been merciful.” Those who have shut up their compassion against the needs of the poor, God will shut up his compassion against; he will let out his fury on them, and they will have their portion in his plagues and indignation, without the least drop of pity or mercy. And at the day of judgment Christ will say to them, Matt 25:41: “Depart from Me, you+ who are cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.” There is their doom. And why? “For I was hungry and you+ gave Me nothing to eat, I was thirsty and you+ gave Me nothing to drink.” Oh, dreadful sentence! Every word of it carries great terror in it and breathes nothing but fire and brimstone. What! Must they depart from Christ, the fountain of bliss and happiness? And into eternal fire? Ah, wretches! Cursed indeed. For as the prophet says in Isa 33:14, “Who of us can dwell with a consuming fire? Who of us can dwell with everlasting burnings?” An everlasting fever, or even an everlasting toothache, would be an unspeakable misery. But what are these compared with lying in that lake which burns with fire and brimstone to all eternity? Oh, I think the very name of eternal fire and everlasting burnings should awaken all uncharitable men out of their complacency, and stir them up without any further delay to mourn their past unmercifulness, to beg pardon for it, and sincerely to resolve to give willingly out of their store toward the relief of the poor, in proportion to what God has graciously given them. It may be that you have a plentiful portion of this world’s goods. But oh, what will it profit you to live plentifully here, and to be eternally miserable hereafter? I truly cannot help standing amazed when I consider how men who believe the words of Christ to be true, that all uncharitable men will be sentenced by him at the last day to everlasting burning for not feeding the hungry and not clothing the naked, can yet be so hardhearted as not to listen to the cry of the poor.

(3.) The misery of uncharitable persons appears in this: the poverty and needs of the poor cry loudly to heaven against them. God has dealt bountifully with you, loading you with his benefits (as the psalmist says, Ps 68:19). He has given you not only food and clothing, things needful and necessary, but an abundance, a plenty of outward things, even all things richly to enjoy. But how many of Christ’s ministers and members are in great want, without the means to satisfy their own and their children’s hunger? Their miseries, like the blood of Abel, cry to God for vengeance against you, saying, “Lord, there are many who have enough and to spare, a generous portion of this world’s goods; like Dives they feast sumptuously every day. But what are we, Your servants in want, the better for them? Which of us is warmed by their fires, or clothed with their garments, or even shares in the crumbs from their table? We are ready to perish for want, while they are glutted with their abundance. Is the blessing of those who are ready to perish likely to come upon them? Will You not judge them, O Lord?” Certainly these bitter and pitiful complaints cry loudly in the ears of the Almighty against such unchristian and inhuman misers. Beware of the cry of the poor against you+. If you will not hear their cries to you, God will hear their cries against you.

(4.) Your unmercifulness to the poor will provoke God to reject your most religious exercises. Prov 21:13: “Whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor, he too shall cry out and receive no answer.” In these words Solomon hints to us two things.

[1.] That unmerciful men, who turn their ears away from the cry of the poor, will fall into such miseries as will bring them to their knees and make them cry out, sooner or later. Here in this world, worldly men sometimes say many prayers, and they hope their religion will make amends, at least for their inhumanity. And in the world to come they will follow their fellow Dives in his devotions in hell.

[2.] Though they cry, yet they will not be heard. Whether they cry here on their deathbeds for mercy, or hereafter in hell for relief, they will not be heard. We have a notable instance of this in Dives. Though he did not cry here, yet he cried in hell, saying, “Father Abraham, have mercy on me and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue. For I am in agony in this fire” (Luke 16:24). But was he heard? Was his request granted? It was only a small request, and yet it is denied. Because he denied crumbs of bread to the poor here in this life, he was denied a drop of water in hell.1

And as your prayers are rejected by God, so too it will be in vain for you to hear the word or to come to the table of the Lord. Shall I say that all your religion will be in vain? No, more than that, it will be an abomination to the Lord, as long as that accursed thing, your covetous and cruel heart, which the Lord abhors (Ps 10:3), remains within you. Do not think that one duty will excuse the neglect of another: that your praying may serve instead of your alms, that religion will excuse your lack of mercy, or that your confessing your unmercifulness will make up for it. The Lord abhors you and all your sacrifices as long as the sacrifice of a compassionate heart is missing.

Oh, that all uncharitable persons would steep their thoughts in a serious meditation on these things! And as they desire to escape the judgments that follow all merciless men, I wish they would put in for a share in the mercies of the merciful. To that end, I wish they would put on hearts of pity and compassion toward the needs and miseries of God’s distressed ones, and stretch out a helping hand toward their relief. This leads me to a second use, namely,

1. The 1676 printing adds here: Non habuit guttam, quia non dedit micam. Aust. (“He did not have a drop, because he did not give a crumb”: Augustine.)

A Use of Exhortation

2. A use of exhortation, to stir up everyone who has given his name to Christ to make conscience of every duty he commands, and of this one especially, which he has pressed on us so earnestly in his word, and encouraged us to by many sweet and precious promises. This work of charity is wages, and like Samson’s lion it carries honey in its belly. The man who, out of a principle of love and in obedience to God’s command, opens his heart and hand wide to the poor will find God blessing his stock and store and prospering all his undertakings. A secret curse goes out from God on the uncharitable man’s estate, which blights all his plans and undertakings, so that they come to nothing. In the same way, a secret blessing goes out from God on the charitable man’s estate, by which he thrives and prospers in the world, to the wonder of himself and his neighbors.

It is observed that the richest merchants and citizens are those who trade boldly, while those who are afraid to venture their goods have only small returns. In the same way experience shows that the Christians who are most ready to supply the needs of the poor, boldly venturing their goods upon the waters, are the ones who thrive and prosper most in the world. Why then will any man be so unwise as to lose his riches for fear of losing them? Why will he not rather seem to lose them, so that he may truly find them? These earthly things are surely lost by keeping them, and kept by bestowing them well.

What remains now but that you+ look about you+ for where you+ may lay out your+ money to your+ best advantage? Make diligent inquiry after the poor ministers and members of Christ; seek them more than they seek you+. For it is most certain that you+ gain more by giving to them than they do by receiving from you+. And you+ are more indebted to them for receiving your+ charity than they are to you+ for giving it. While you+ only relieve their bodies, they feed your+ souls, as in Prov 11:17: “A merciful man benefits his own soul,” which is refreshed by the mercy he shows to others. And while they share in a small quantity of your+ outward good things, you+ will have the same in kind returned here sevenfold into your+ bosoms. And at last you+ will be received into the kingdom of heaven, prepared for all those who have fed the hungry, clothed the naked, and done such works of charity to the poor members of Christ (Matt 25:35). So you+ do not benefit the poor so much by giving as you+ profit yourselves+ by receiving.

Riches are a sheer uncertainty, like a flock of birds in a man’s field: he cannot say they are his because they sit there; for wealth “makes wings for itself and flies.” Now in dealing with uncertain things, it will be your+ wisdom,

  1. To make them as sure as you+ can.
  2. To make the best use of them that you+ can.

(1.) What greater wisdom is there than to make sure? And what better way can be imagined to make your+ estate sure than by putting it into good hands? And what hands are safer than the hands of the Lord? Put your+ riches into the hands of God’s poor, and by doing so you+ put them into God’s hands.

In the affairs of a state, the resident ambassadors who are sent abroad to live in foreign kingdoms secure our peace at home. So what we give out and send out to the poor secures the rest at home. For as the poor beg of you, so they beg of God for you, that he would preserve and bless your store. Their prayers are sent up to heaven for your security.

(2.) And what better use can you+ make of your+ riches than to bestow a part of them on the poor and needy? For it is the chief end of God’s giving more of this world’s goods to some than to others, that those who have the greater store should give out of it to those who are in want. This was typified in the Israelites’ gathering of the manna. Though it was rained down from heaven, yet the Lord would not allow those who had gathered more than was needed for themselves and their household to hoard up their surplus. He commanded them to share their abundance with those who did not have enough, so that the man who had the most should have nothing left over, and the man who had the least should have no lack. The apostle applies this to the giving of alms out of our abundance to those who are in want (2 Cor 8:14).

By sharing our riches with the poor, we will make them our friends, both to give evidence for us of the truth of our faith and charity, and to beg a plentiful return on us. This is the advice of our Savior in Luke 16:9: “Make friends for yourselves+ by means of the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when you+ fail, they will receive you+ into eternal dwellings.” Here by mammon our Savior means the abundance of this world’s goods. He called it the mammon of unrighteousness because worldly men ordinarily get it unrighteously, keep it unrighteously, and use it unrighteously. He hints at this so that his disciples might be all the more wary of it, and all the more careful about making themselves friends by it. That is, they should so use their riches in relieving the poor that the good works done by them may give testimony of their faith and charity, which is the part of friends. Friends are ready to give good testimony of one another. The coats and garments that Dorcas made for poor widows (Acts 9:39) were such friends. But note what follows: Make friends for yourselves+ by means of the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when you+ fail, they will receive you+ into eternal dwellings. When you+ fail, that is, when you+ depart out of this world, they will receive you+ into eternal dwellings. Some refer this word they to those who, being relieved, call on God to recompense their benefactors; but most refer it to the riches which the givers bestow on the poor. Because of the evidence these riches give of the faith and charity of the giver, they are said to receive the givers into eternal dwellings.

Surely rich men have a price in their hands with which to purchase a good inheritance for themselves, if only they had hearts to make use of it. Though charity lays no claim to any merit ex congruo, or condigno [of fitness, or of worthiness], yet it will be plentifully rewarded by God both here and hereafter.

I hope you+ will pardon my zeal in pressing this duty of charity on you+ so much. I assure you+ it does not come from any design to take anything from yourselves+ and your+ children, but only to show you+ the surest and safest way of thriving in the world, and how you+ may settle God’s blessing on your+ children, and so secure for them the portion you+ leave them. I am willing to do you+ a kindness, and I will do you+ a great kindness if I can only persuade you+ effectually to this duty. Whatever kindness I may do in this to those in need, I will do a greater kindness to you+ who will be persuaded to help them in their need, inasmuch as it is more blessed to give than to receive. So bear with me if I not only offer you+ a kindness, but press you+ so earnestly to accept it.

The apostle, knowing how reluctant rich men especially were in all works of charity, advises Timothy (1 Tim 6:17) not only to commend the duty to them, but to command it. The apostle’s expression is well worth noting. He does not say ἀγγέλλε, declare to them, but παράγγελλε, charge those who are rich in this world, as they love their lives and would save their souls, to be rich in good works. As one wittily comments on those words of the apostle: If God should charge the rocks, they would send out water; if the stones, they would become bread; if the ravens, they would feed Elijah; if the quails, they would feed the camp; if the clouds, they would rain down food from heaven on his poor people. Will you+ then be more rocky than rocks? More stony than stones? More ravenous than ravens? More senseless than birds? More empty than clouds?

If you+ are rich in this world’s goods and are not rich in good works, do not talk of your+ faith, for there can be no true faith without good works (Jas 2:17). And do not tell me of your+ religion, for there can be no true religion in you+ as long as you+ make no conscience of this duty. “Pure … religion,” says the apostle James (Jas 1:27), “is this: to care for orphans and widows in their distress”; and you+ never learned any other religion from us.

The Lord does indeed give us leave to eat and drink, and to cheer our hearts by enjoying, in some measure, the portion he has given us. But he never allowed us to keep it all to ourselves, or to spend it in gratifying our sinful lusts. He commands us to set apart some portion of our estate for the relief of those for whom nothing is provided. Prov 3:9: “Honor the Lord with your wealth,” says the wise man. He does not say, Honor yourself with your riches, but honor the Lord with them. As they come from his grace, so they should be used for his glory. Now we use our riches for God’s glory when, in obedience to his command, we supply with them the needs of his children, who will be stirred up by this to bless and praise the name of God for his fatherly care and providence over them.

Do I need to tell you yet again that your liberality to the poor cannot bring any loss to your estate, since the more you give, the more you will receive? It is told in fable of Midas that whatever he touched was turned into gold. But it is no fable or fancy that the hand of charity can do it: it can draw grace out of your+ goods, righteousness out of riches, and heaven out of earth. Giving away goods to such good uses, while it seems to impair what you+ have, mightily improves it, to your+ most singular advantage. The more generous any man is, the more likely he is to be a rich man. The mercy of God will crown his kindness with such a blessing of store that he will find God will never be behindhand with him. What the poor receive from him is nothing in comparison with the blessing he will receive from the Lord. It may be that you do not find your store increased at once by it. Yet if you diligently observe the workings of God’s providence toward you, you will sooner or later find yourself abundantly repaid for all that you have paid out.

Directions for Giving

I told you+ before that I am willing to do you+ a kindness. And so that it may be a kindness indeed, I must tell you+ further not only what you+ should do, but how you+ must do it, so that you+ may not lose your+ reward. And if you+ want to make sure of being gainers by whatever you+ lay out in this way, observe the following DIRECTIONS.

I. Give yourselves to the Lord, and with yourselves all that you have, to be laid out, whether on yourselves or on others, as he appoints and requires.

2 Cor 8:2. The apostle, boasting of the Macedonian Christians and of the riches of their liberality, tells us in v. 5 that they gave themselves first to the Lord. The man who will not give himself to the Lord is likely to give little else. And if he should give all that he had, and withhold only himself, God will not accept it or reward it. God will have nothing of you if he may not have your heart.

Give yourselves+ to the Lord as servants, to serve him with your+ spirits first, and then with all that you+ have. Make yourselves+ over to God in Christ to be his covenant servants, and from then on count and say of yourselves+, as the apostle teaches you+ (1 Cor 6:20), I am not my own, but must from now on glorify God with my body and my spirit, yes, and with all that I have, which are his.

The man who says I serve the Lord, and has not first given himself to him as a servant, does not know what he is saying; God will not be served by aliens. And the man who says I give myself to the Lord as a servant, and does not actually serve him with all that he has, has only lied to God. The man who has given himself to the Lord will withhold nothing from him that God will have.

The man who will serve the Lord with his spirit will just as readily serve him with all that he has. God, who has given us his Son, “how will He not also, along with Him, freely give us all things?” (Rom 8:32). And the man who has given God his soul will keep nothing back from him.

Friend, you say you are the Lord’s and have devoted yourself to him. You hope that you are Christ’s, and have joined yourself to him in covenant, resolving to be his disciple. But which way does your estate run? Whose is this house, these lands, and this money that you have? Are these the Lord’s too? How is it, then, that your lusts have so much of them at their service? That your pride has so much, and your appetite so much? Or that they are all taken over and kept by you to feed your covetousness? Is all you have the Lord’s? How is it, then, that you begrudge every little thing he calls for from you, or think it too much? You who will not, in every case, part with as much as God calls for, are either a liar or a robber. Either you did not give all to God when you said you did, and then you are a liar; or if you did give all, and yet will not let him have what he calls for but bestow it elsewhere, then you are a robber.

Objection. But some will say, “Must I give all I have to the poor, and so leave myself and my family to be beggars? Or what else do you mean when you say I must give all to the Lord?”

My meaning is this: that you so give all to the Lord as to resolve to dispose of your whole estate to such persons and purposes as God orders and appoints for you. The Lord would have you live and maintain yourself, and provide for your family soberly, according to your rank and station (some extraordinary cases excepted). But still you must allow no more to yourself, and no less to those in need, than accords with the will and good pleasure of the Lord.

Someone else will put in here and say, “But I am generous and bountiful, and give great alms. I cast my bread upon the waters; I give a portion to six, and also to seven. I devise liberal things; I delight to show mercy.”

Do you? It is well that you do; God’s blessing on your heart for it. It would be a great pity for any generous man in the world to lose his reward. And so that you may not lose yours, take this counsel from a friend who loves you. See that you have sincerely given yourself up to God as his covenant servant, and are a devoted disciple of Jesus Christ. See that these works of mercy of yours are done in keeping with your covenant, as a part of the service that you owe and have vowed to your Lord, whose you are, and whose talents you count all that you have. And look to this all the more because it is possible that men of great good works may be men of little charity, and of little faith also. And faith is the grace that gives God his right to us and to all we do, and obtains our acceptance with him. First by faith give yourself to him, and then by charity serve him with what you have, and then do not doubt of a plentiful return.

II. Offer up your+ gift on the altar. Give yourselves+, and with yourselves+ all that you+ have, through Christ, to God. Let him be your+ altar that sanctifies your+ gift. It is through him alone that you+ will be accepted: “He has made us accepted in the Beloved One” (Eph 1:6). Let your+ souls be sprinkled with his blood, and so washed from your+ blood, from your+ natural and acquired guilt and pollution; and then they will be a gift acceptable to the Lord. Do not think you+ have nothing more to do than to give yourselves+ to the Lord as you+ are. You+ have given yourselves+ to sin, and now perhaps you+ think you+ will give yourselves+ back to the Lord; but know that there is more to it than that. You are in yourself a guilty and defiled soul, and God will have none of you in this state. Go to Christ first, and get him to cover your unrighteousness and to cleanse you from your filthiness. Put your wretched soul into his hands, and let him present it to the Father.

And whatever you give along with yourself for his poor, your alms, your bread, or your flesh, or your money, put it all into the same hand, and let him present this also to the Father, for the use of his servants.

Friends, though I would have you+ be givers, yet I would not have you+ be losers. I would not have you+ be losers either by saving or by unprofitable giving.

(1.) Do not be losers by saving. That is the quickest way to lose all: thinking to save and keep all to yourselves. “Whoever wants to save his life” (that is, by not laying it down when God calls for it) “will lose it.” And so whoever wants to save his estate, that is, by refusing to lay it out where God would have him, is all the more likely to lose all that he has.

(2.) Do not lose by unprofitable giving. Everything is given unprofitably, as far as you are concerned, whoever you give it to, if it is not given first through Christ to God, and to his servants for the Lord’s sake. It may still be a profit to those who receive it, but it is no profit to you who give. It is only what is given to God, and to men for God’s sake, for which God becomes a debtor.

III. Fetch all your+ alms out of your+ hearts. “Draw out your soul to the hungry” (Isa 58:10). Give what you give 1, out of a willing heart; 2, out of a compassionate heart; 3, out of a thankful heart.

(1.) Out of a willing heart; give willingly. 2 Cor 9:7: “Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver.” An alms-deed is called in Scripture a sacrifice, a sacrifice that is well pleasing to God (Heb 13:16): “Do not neglect to do good and to share with others, for with such sacrifices God is pleased.” Now all our Christian sacrifices are to be freewill offerings. An alms without a will is a sacrifice without a heart, and will be rejected by God.

(2.) Out of a compassionate heart. Get a compassionate heart, and fetch all your alms out of your own heart. It is the hard hearts of men that shut up their purses. You say you have nothing to spare: you need it yourself, or those around you may need it. No, you lack a heart, and that is the reason those in need must go without your alms. A compassionate heart would find something or other for those who are in distress.

Get a compassionate heart. God is a God of compassion, and his children are compassionate children. Col 3:12: “As the elect of God, … clothe yourselves with hearts of compassion.” 1 John 3:17: “If anyone with earthly possessions sees his brother in need, but withholds his compassion from him” (or is a man without compassion), “how can the love of God abide in him?” Whatever your profession of faith or your religion may be, or your hopes concerning it, you have nothing of God in you; you are none of his, if you have no compassion. God is a God of mercy; his children are all merciful children.

Worldling, will you prove yourself to be no child of God? Would you prove that the faith you have is vain, your religion vain, and that you are only a pretender to the love of God, and do not have the love of God within you? This unmercifulness of yours will put it beyond question. If you have no compassion, the love of God is not in you.

O get a compassionate and merciful heart. Have you received mercy, and will you not be merciful? Do you hope for mercy, and will you not show mercy? Put yourself in your poor brother’s place for a while. Think how hard it is with him; think of his hunger and nakedness, of his pressing straits and miseries. Let your soul go into his house and see his bare walls, his cold fireplace, his empty cupboard, his starving children. And then think again: O what if it were like this with me! Ah, poor distressed creatures, how they are pinched and starved, while I have enough and abound! O my compassion, how can you not yearn? O my heart, how can you not bleed over such distressed ones? Have you nothing to help them? There is enough in my house, there is enough in my purse to give them relief; but is there no alms for them in my heart? Can I have the heart to see them starve and perish, and do nothing to help them? Where are you, O my pity? Where are my compassions? O my soul, help, and send portions to those for whom nothing is provided.

(3.) Out of a thankful heart. Remember what God has done for you. Have you any sense or experience of his special love to you in Christ? What should that produce? The sense of divine goodness in the way of common providence calls for all due acknowledgment from us. But a taste of his fatherly love in pardoning our sins, justifying our persons, and bringing us into the possession of eternal life and happiness, on account of his Son’s suffering and dying for us, is both the strongest motive to our charity, or kindness, to our fellow creatures who stand in need of it, and the most commanding reason for it.

In Christ the beams of God’s mercy are gathered to a point, as the beams of the sun are in a burning glass. As they fall on our hearts, our hearts are, or should be, set on fire by them, and made to burn with a greater heat of love and kindness to all in want, especially to all who bear his image. The right spring of mercy to our neighbor is the sense of God’s mercy toward us.

IV. Let all your+ streams of love flow into the ocean. My meaning is, let all be done to the glory of God. This must be your+ final end, to which all must be directed, as the apostle charges in 1 Cor 10:31: “Whether you+ eat or drink” (I may add, or whether you+ give to eat or to drink) “or whatever you+ do, do it all to the glory of God.” Let this be chiefly in your+ eye and your+ heart: that God may be glorified. There are other, subordinate ends, such as the refreshing of the needy, the adorning of our holy profession of faith, and the edification of others by our good example; but all must at last end here, that God may be glorified.

Take care that your+ end is not to glorify yourselves+. As worms breed in the fairest fruit, so pride and vainglory are apt to creep up out of the best duties.

V. Let your+ works of charity be done in humility, giving God the honor of them, by acknowledging that what you+ have bestowed on the poor you+ first received from him, and that it was his goodness that gave you+ a heart to give anything out of your+ abundance toward their relief. Indeed, you+ ought always to keep a close watch over yourselves+, in case there has been some hypocrisy and self-seeking in your+ works of charity. Acknowledge that you+ are so far from meriting heaven and salvation by your+ good works that, if God should deal with you+ according to the rigor of his justice, he might cast you+ into hell for the pride and hypocrisy that cling to your+ best works.

VI. Let your+ works of charity to men be accompanied with prayers and thanksgivings to God. Thank God that he has put you+ among the givers and not among the receivers, since “it is more blessed to give than to receive”; that he has put you+ among the givers and not the withholders; that he has given you+ an estate to give and a heart to give. Thank God that he will accept a gift at your+ hands: that he, to whom all you+ have belongs, and to whom it is owed, will count as a gift what is only the payment of so small a part of your+ debt. Say with David in 1 Chronicles 29:11, 13: “Yours, O Lord, is the greatness … Both riches and honor come from You … Now therefore, our God, we give You thanks, and we praise Your glorious name. But who am I, and who are my people, that we should be able to give as generously as this? For everything comes from You, and from Your own hand we have given to You.”

VII. Give out in proportion to what God has given to you+, 1 Cor 16:2. The apostle advises the Corinthians to give as God had prospered them.

Rich men, therefore, ought to be rich in good works, for God expects fruit to match the seed that he sows. Has he abounded toward you+ in this world’s goods? Then you+ ought to be abundant in good works toward others. Your+ pounds are expected, where the widow’s mites are accepted.

The Means of This Grace

Having given you+ some directions for the manner of giving your+ alms, I will briefly show you+ the means by which you+ may attain this grace of Christian charity.

Now the means I will prescribe will be of two kinds:

  1. Those that tend to bring your+ hearts to be willing to do this duty.
  2. Those that tend to help you+ to manage it better.

1. First, as means to bring your+ hearts to be willing to set about this duty, take these.

Often call to mind, and print in your+ memories, the many precepts in the Scriptures that require this duty at your+ hands; and also the many gracious promises God has made there to encourage his people in it. And then reason with yourself like this: What? Has God commanded me to give to my brother according to his need (Deut 15:10)? To cast my bread upon the waters (Eccl 11:1)? And has our blessed Savior commanded me to give to the poor (Luke 6:38)?

And has the Lord, to encourage me in it, promised that he will bless me in all my works, and prosper me in all that I put my hand to, in my trade and calling? That my barns will be filled with plenty? That what we give or lend to the poor, he will pay us back with interest? That though I cast my bread upon the waters, where it may seem to be lost, yet I will find it after many days, and it will certainly be returned into my bosom with increase? And has my Savior, to encourage me, promised that if I give to the poor, it will be given to me again, good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, running over (Luke 6:38)? Then certainly there is no shorter way to thrive and prosper in the world than by my liberality to the poor.

(2.) Prefer heaven and the things of heaven to this earth and earthly things. Though the temporal reward I have dwelt on so much is a great encouragement, yet the greatest encouragement is the spiritual and eternal reward the Lord has promised. And so that this encouragement may prevail the more, learn to esteem and prize things spiritual and eternal above all things that are only temporal. Suppose it should happen that you+ never receive back in kind what you+ give; yet count those temporal things sold at the best price when what you+ receive for them is spiritual and eternal. Value grace and glory above all the treasures of the earth, and count yourselves+ to grow rich men as you+ abound in grace and in your+ evidences for glory. And count it an unthrifty saving and holding back when you+ have an opportunity to gain in your+ inner man by spending your+ outward wealth.

Until heaven is valued above earth, this great argument encouraging acts of bounty and mercy will lose its efficacy. When God says, “Cast your bread upon the waters, for after many days you will find it again,” the worldling will be ready to ask, But how will I find it? In what way will it be returned to me? Will I have bread for bread, or money for my bread, or houses or lands for my money? Very likely you may. But suppose not; yet it will be better than that. You will have in grace what you part with in bread or money; you will reap in heaven what you sow on the waters.

Yes, but the worldling will reply, I do not mean to part with my bread or my money that way. No, I know you do not; but the reason is that you love this earth more than heaven. You say, Will grace feed me? Will grace clothe me? Can I keep myself and my family? Can we live and be maintained, and be kept from poverty and beggary here, by hopes of glory hereafter?

Go, fool, and learn better what God is, and what his everlasting mercy is. Let the lasting treasures, the durable riches, be prized and valued more by you, and this will stop your mouth and silence your heart from such vain reasonings. You will never again say, I cannot spare my bread or my money, when you see that by spending it for God you make him your debtor, who will pay it back to you in spiritual and eternal good things, once you count these better than your bread or your money.

But until you have come to be settled in this judgment and belief, both that the good things of God are infinitely better than the good things of this earth, and that what you sow on earth you will certainly reap in heaven, until you come in good earnest to be of this mind, God’s poor are likely to be little the better for you.

It is this, beloved, that will effectually do it, that will open your+ hearts and open your+ hands in bounty and liberality for God: when you+ come to be rooted in the practical belief of this principle, on which the practice of all religion stands and is upheld in the world, that heaven is better than earth; and if this other is added to it, that what is sincerely laid out for God on earth will certainly be repaid in heaven; besides the return which the Lord often makes to the charitable here in this world.

2. For the means that tend to help you+ manage it better, take these that follow.

(1.) Either follow the example of the early saints, in setting apart something every Lord’s day out of the past week’s earnings.

Or, 2. Devote to God a certain portion of your yearly income for charitable uses.

That the former way, setting apart something every Lord’s day for the relief of the poor, was the practice of the early Christians is clear from the apostle’s words to the Corinthians (1 Cor 16:1, 2): “Now about the collection for the saints, you+ are to do as I directed the churches of Galatia. On the first day of every week” (which is the Lord’s day) “each of you+ should set aside a portion and save it up, as God has prospered him.” This way and course concerns in particular those who live on their daily labor.

But to gentlemen and others who live on their rents and official posts, and to merchants and citizens who balance their accounts once a year, I would commend the latter way: to devote to God a certain portion of their yearly income, by rent or otherwise, and then, separating it from the rest, to count it a sacred stock for the poor, not to be used for any other purpose.

All men by nature (through the corruption that is in them) are hard-hearted and close-handed, very unwilling to part with anything considerable for charitable uses when an occasion comes suddenly. But when they have set something apart beforehand, their ears, hearts and hands are open to every charitable appeal, and they are very ready and eager to give to it the more liberally out of what is laid by, rejoicing that they have met with so good an object of charity.

As for the quota pars, what proportion every one ought to set apart out of his yearly income for good uses, I do not find it particularly set down in the word of God, and therefore I dare not positively determine it. All the more so because there are so many circumstances that alter the case that no certain rule can be given. I will leave it to the discretion and honest judgment of the prudent Christian.

But though the Scripture does not determine the exact proportion to be set apart for good works, yet it does command us to give in proportion to what God has given us; to open our hands wide to the needs of the poor; to be rich in good works, and the like. Yes, the Scripture commends to us the examples of very bountiful Christians: of Dorcas, of whom it is said that she “was always occupied with works of kindness and charity” (Acts 9:36); of Cornelius, of whom it is said that he “gave generously to the people” (Acts 10:2); and of the Macedonians, of whom it is said that “they gave according to their ability and even beyond it” (2 Cor 8:3). It likewise commends to us the example of Jacob, who, in testimony of his thankfulness to God for what God would give him, vowed the tenth of it to God for pious and charitable uses, as in Gen 28:20, 22: “Then Jacob made a vow, saying, … ‘Of all that You give me I will surely give You a tenth.’ ”

These examples are left on record for us to imitate; for as the apostle says, “everything that was written in the past was written for our instruction” (Rom 15:4), and for our admonition. Most of those I have heard or read of who have taken this course, consecrating to God a certain portion of their wealth for charitable uses, have followed the example of Jacob in giving a tenth part to God. And as God greatly blessed Jacob after his vow, so he has likewise blessed very many others after a like vow to God.

Mr. Stock, in his funeral sermon at the burial of Lord Harrington, speaking of his charity, declared that in his lifetime he gave the tenth part of his yearly revenue to the poor. Mr. Gataker, in his funeral sermon at the burial of Mr. John Parker, merchant and citizen of London, speaking of his charity, says that at his first effectual call, among other things he then resolved on, this was one: to set apart every year a tenth of his gain for the relief of the poor and needy; and that from that time God abundantly advanced his estate. And no doubt, if those merchants who usually insure their goods when they fear danger at sea would sincerely promise to God, in testimony of their thankfulness to him, the tenth of what came safe into their hands, they might receive far greater returns than they do.

In the life of Dr. Hammond, written by Dr. Fell, I find this statement: “The rate and sum of what the doctor devoted was the tenth of all his income, and in this he was so strictly exact that commonly the first thing he did was to compute and set apart the poor man’s share.” And how his stock increased, notwithstanding his abundant giving for the relief of others, the history declares at length. I read the like in the life of Mr. William Wheatly, minister of Banbury: how for many years he set apart the tenth of his yearly income, from both his temporal and his ecclesiastical revenues, and that his estate prospered the better after he took that course. To these I could add many more out of the lives of good and charitable men, and out of various funeral sermons which are printed and published. And I could name multitudes of men now living who have devoted a like or greater portion of their wealth to charitable uses, and are ready to attest the truth of this discourse, that they are no losers, but great gainers in temporal things, by what they have given to the poor.

Mr. Richard Baxter, in his learned and useful work called A Christian Directory, part 4, fol. 195, on the quota pars, what proportion is fit for most men to devote to charitable uses, and whether the tenth part of their increase is not ordinarily a fit proportion, has this statement:

Though the proportion of the tenth part is too much for some, and much too little for others, yet for the most part I think it as suitable a proportion as it is fit for another to prescribe in particular.

Yet I would not be thought to impose this as a proportion to be kept by all; for not all men’s hearts are equally enlarged with love and bounty. And there are some who have no more than is necessary for the comfortable support of themselves and their family; from them less is required for the relief of others. But I would advise those whom the Lord has blessed with a plentiful estate, so that their necessary expenses are, or might be, far less than their incomes, to devote a tenth part of their whole yearly income to charitable uses. I say, of their whole yearly income, without first deducting any part of it for food, clothes, or other necessary expenses; for the tenth of the remainder would be a very small proportion for a rich man to devote to charity, and far short of what the Scripture seems to call for.

And know for certain that this course is so far from being a means of diminishing your+ stock and store that, if it is managed as it ought to be, according to the rules and directions given before, it is the surest and safest means, the shortest course, of increasing it, through the secret blessing of God which goes with it. This has been sufficiently shown in the foregoing discourse.

(2.) Be careful on whom you bestow your alms. For by giving to common beggars who are able to work, and yet are so lazy that they will not work but would live by the sweat of other men’s brows, I say, by relieving such, we will both maintain them in their idle and wicked life, and neglect those who are truly poor and ought to be looked on as the proper objects of our charity, or at least cut them short of what rightly belongs to them.

I am not against all relieving of beggars. Some of them, I know, are blind, others lame, aged, and past their work. These disabled poor, in view of their present condition, are objects of charity. But not the impudent poor, who have strength enough to work and will not, those canting vagrants who are the burden of the earth and the shame of the kingdom: for these I have no charity. Neither had the apostle St. Paul, who was full of compassion toward God’s poor; but for the devil’s poor he gave this command, “If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat” (2 Thess 3:10), so that hunger and need might drive them to labor. Erasmus mentions a kind of mercy most fit for such: it is misericordia puniens [a mercy that punishes]. Surely the whip is more their due than food, and Bridewell [a house of correction] to receive them rather than an almshouse.

III. Another means for attaining this grace of Christian charity is this: Be earnest with God in prayer, that he would be pleased to give you that adorning and enriching grace of charity, and accept your offering. This sacrifice, as it must be offered up to heaven, so it must be fetched from heaven. The gift of a merciful and charitable heart is one of those gifts that come down from above, from the Father of lights (Jas 1:17). If you do not receive this gift from God, your poor brother is likely to have no gift from you. Now it is your prayer that must fetch down this gift from God. Lift up your heart to the Lord, and beg for a merciful and compassionate soul. Beg God to make you ready for every good work, willing to share with the poor members of Christ according to your ability and their need, so that by this you may lay up in store for yourself a good foundation for the time to come, and so take hold of eternal life. Pray for a willing heart, and pray that your gift may be accepted, that your alms may be such a sacrifice, and so offered up, that the Lord may be well pleased with it.

Having thus shown you+ the means to be performed on our part for attaining and exercising this grace of charity, I will close this discourse by answering two or three objections.

Objection 1. Some plead the size of their household, the number of their children, who must be provided for, and say that they therefore have little to give to the poor.

Answer 1. Do you have many children? Then you ought all the more to be charitable, so that by this you may settle God’s blessing on them, which is the best portion and surest inheritance you can leave them. That will secure their stock and increase their store; whereas unmercifulness to the poor will settle a curse instead of a blessing on the persons and estates of your children.

(2.) You who plead the number of your children as an excuse for your stinginess: how justly may God then lessen the number, and so take away this excuse by taking your children from you!

(3.) Suppose you have many children, perhaps ten; count God as one more, and give him a child’s portion. I mean, give the poor, for his sake, as much every year as one child costs you. Give them a child’s portion, and I dare boldly say you will not be the poorer, but rather a great gainer. For by this you will procure God’s blessing on yourself and your children, which in truth is all in all; and without it, all is likely to come to nothing, as we see by daily experience. This made St. Augustine say, Haeredi praestabis, quicquid misericordiae causa de ejus portione detraxeris, [you will make good to the heir whatever you take from his portion for mercy’s sake] Aug. De Tempore, Serm. 76. What you give out of your estate to charitable uses will be no loss to your children, but rather a great advantage. Yes, the Spirit of God, in setting forth the happiness of a merciful man, says that his children will fare the better for his goodness and bounty, as in Ps 37:26: “He is ever generous and quick to lend, and his children are blessed”; that is, God will bless his children, not only with spiritual but also with temporal blessings.

2. Objection. Many who profess religion in these days are very barren in good works.

Answer. Fruitless and uncharitable Christians may make a profession of religion, but without question they are not sound Christians, nor sincere in their profession. For it is most certain that the elect of God put on hearts of mercy and compassion, as the apostle says (Col 3:12). And therefore an uncharitable Christian is a plain contradiction. For who is a Christian but he who conforms himself to the law and life of Christ? The substance of Christ’s law is charity, and his life was spent in going about doing good, one way or another, to the souls and bodies of men and women.

Therefore whoever has this world’s goods, and sees his brother in need, and shuts up his heart of compassion from him, and will not share anything considerable toward his needs, let his profession of faith be ever so fair and glorious in the eyes of men, yet certainly he is only a rotten professing Christian and a dissembling hypocrite in the sight of God. In Matthew 25:34-36 we find that liberality to the members of Christ is made the special touchstone of true faith and godliness. For the charitable are those who at the great day of judgment will appear as the sheep at Christ’s right hand, and will hear that joyful sentence of absolution: “Come, you+ who are blessed by My Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you+ from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you+ gave Me something to eat, I was thirsty and you+ gave Me something to drink, I was a stranger and you+ took Me in, I was naked and you+ clothed Me, I was sick and you+ looked after Me, I was in prison and you+ visited Me.”

And on the other side, all unmerciful men who have not relieved Christ in his members, whatever profession of religion they have made here in this world, will yet appear at the last day as the goats set at Christ’s left hand, and will hear that dreadful sentence of condemnation: “Depart from Me, you+ who are cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry and you+ gave Me nothing to eat, I was thirsty and you+ gave Me nothing to drink, I was a stranger and you+ did not take Me in, naked and you+ did not clothe Me, sick and in prison and you+ did not visit Me.” Hence it appears that, as mercy and bounty to the poor members of Christ is a conspicuous evidence of true faith and sincere godliness in a Christian, and clearly declares him godly, so stinginess and unmercifulness to them is a clear mark of unbelief and ungodliness, and clearly declares him to be an unbeliever, and so a wicked and profane person. Therefore I would much question the sincerity of the faith and piety of those who make a profession of religion and yet show little or no charity to the poor members of Christ. For as the apostle James says (Jas 1:27), “Pure and undefiled religion before our God and Father is this: to care for orphans and widows in their distress.” This implies that works of mercy and charity rightly performed are clear evidences of the truth of our religion and the sincerity of our profession of faith. And if you+ look into the Scriptures, you+ will scarcely read of a man truly godly without reading also that he was merciful and charitable, eager in every good work.

So much will suffice for this point of doctrine.

A Word for the Ministers

A word or two, for my brethren’s sake, on the first doctrine drawn from the foregoing verse, which is the principal point our Savior intends there. It was this:

1. That all needful help and good hospitality ought to be given in particular to the ministers of the Gospel.

Our Savior, in commending objects to our charity, mentions prophets and righteous ones in the first place, saying, “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward”; and then he adds, “whoever receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man,” etc.

Indeed, our charity must be so general in its extent and reach that it does not exclude any who are in want and distress. For though we may, and ought to, make a difference between the men on whom we bestow our charity, yet we ought not to withhold it from any men who are in want; we must exercise the grace of charity toward those who do not have the grace of faith. Yes, “let us do good to everyone,” as the apostle exhorts (Gal 6:10), “and especially to the family of faith”; and among them, chiefly to the ministers of Christ. So this object of charity, the prophet, is not to be taken here exclusively, but by way of eminence and preference: ministers are to be ministered to before and above others, with more readiness and cheerfulness.

We read that the people of Israel were commanded again and again not to leave or forsake their Levites, especially when the Levites were brought into any straits and difficulties (Deut 12:19; 14:27). Much less, then, should the ministers of the Gospel be left and forsaken by the people of God when they lie under any want or distress.

The examples of God’s people who have gone before us in performing this duty are many, both in the Old Testament and in the New. It is recorded to the lasting praise and commendation of Obadiah that he hid the prophets of God by fifties in a cave from the cruelty of Jezebel, and sustained them with food, and supplied them with all things necessary (1 Kgs 18:13). We read likewise how the widow of Zarephath fed the prophet Elijah in her house for many days and years, as long as the famine lasted (1 Kgs 17:15, 16). The kindness of the good Shunammite to the prophet Elisha is told at length (2 Kgs 4:8, etc.): “One day Elisha went to Shunem, and a prominent woman who lived there persuaded him to eat bread”; that is, to refresh himself with food. “So whenever he would pass by, he would stop there to eat.” Having found good hospitality and a hearty welcome, he visited the family the more often. “Then the woman said to her husband, ‘Behold, now I know that the one who often comes our way is a holy man of God. Please let us make a small room on the wall and put in it a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp for him.’ ” Under these, other necessary comforts are included. The good woman asked her husband that a room might be made for the prophet on the wall; perhaps not because she lacked room in her house to lodge him, but because she considered that the noise of a great household might disturb the prophet’s study and devotion. Therefore she thought it fitting to provide such a room for him, where he might be more retired and free to come and go, so that by those comforts he might be encouraged to lodge there the more often.

It is set down as the height and crown of Phoebe’s good works (Rom 16:2) that she had been a helper of the apostle Paul in his needs and straits. And in 2 Timothy 1:16 we read how Onesiphorus refreshed and relieved the apostle in his suffering condition, and was not ashamed of his chains; that is, though Paul was a prisoner, and under restraint for the gospel’s sake, yet Onesiphorus was not ashamed of him, showed him all respect, and helped and relieved him in that low condition. Gaius likewise, a godly, wealthy citizen of Corinth, is famous for the kind hospitality and help he gave to the apostle and the church with him (Rom 16:23).

It is recorded to the commendation of King Edward the Sixth that he gave all needful help and good hospitality to Bucer, Fagius, and other divines, when they fled into this kingdom because of the troubles in their own nation. And Beza, in his epistle ad Regem Jacobum [to King James], makes honorable mention of a liberal collection from the church of Scotland sent to the French ministers who were banished religionis causa [for the sake of religion].

Here are fair copies for us to write after. And indeed, why are these things written and left on record to posterity, if not for our learning? Not so much for our admiration as for our imitation, that we might follow their steps and write after their copy. St. Paul testifies this of the Macedonians (2 Cor 9:2): that very many of them were stirred up and provoked to a liberal contribution to the poor saints at Jerusalem by the eagerness and zeal of the Corinthians. And St. Augustine (Confes. Lib. 9. cap. 2.) confesses that the examples of God’s servants burned up and consumed his own lukewarmness, and their fervent zeal set an edge on his devotion.

To these examples I will add a few reasons, to press this duty on you+ the more.

Reason I. Because ministers, when they are supported, are likely to be most serviceable to the church of God. They are spiritual fathers, to beget men to Christ. They are his ambassadors, and stand in his place to reveal the mysteries of the kingdom, sent out to be reconcilers between God and this sinful world, to pray and beseech men to be reconciled to God (2 Cor 5:20). Their work is to bear the name of God, to publish the salvation of God before the world, to open the eyes of the blind, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among those who are sanctified. In this respect ministers of the Gospel are more useful and serviceable in their generation than lawyers, physicians or tradesmen, who are yet useful enough.

(1.) Lawyers indeed may be a means of settling your+ right to your+ goods and lands; but ministers, of settling your+ right to your+ heavenly inheritance.

(2.) Physicians may cure the illnesses of your+ bodies; but ministers are sent to cure the diseases of your+ souls.

(3.) Merchants and all sorts of tradesmen may stock a land with all kinds of goods necessary for this life; but ministers alone bring in such heavenly and spiritual treasures as spring up into everlasting treasure.

So by supplying the ministers’ bodily needs you+ comfort and refresh the souls of many. And what better charity can be imagined than, by relieving the temporal needs of a few, to further the everlasting salvation of many? Oh, what cause they will have to bless God to all eternity for your+ charity, those who have been converted by the ministry of the men you+ have refreshed and supported in their work!

Reason II. Another reason may be taken from considering the quality of the persons for whom I am pleading: they are not so lowly as they outwardly appear. Those whom you+ see so poorly clothed, walking so dejectedly, without many outward comforts, are men endowed with many singular prerogatives and privileges, not only above the rest of God’s people, but also above the most glorious angels.

Compare them first with the people of God. The people are called the Lord’s sheep; the ministers, the shepherds of the flock (Ezek 34:2). The people are children in God’s family; the ministers are spiritual fathers, who beget men to God by the seed of the word (1 Cor 4:15). Therefore the Spirit of God grants them this dignity, to be called συνεργοὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ, fellow laborers with God.

As for angels, it is true that they and ministers are fellow servants (Rev 22:9). But ministers still have various prerogatives above them.

(1.) Angels rejoice at the conversion of a sinner (Luke 15:10). But it is by the ministry of prophets that sinners are converted to God (Acts 26:18).

(2.) An angel was sent to Cornelius to tell him where to go to be instructed; but a minister instructed him in the way of life (Acts 10:6, 34).

(3.) Was the word of reconciliation ever committed to angels? It is committed to ministers (2 Cor 5:18). It is worth noting that what ministers carry as ambassadors is not simply ἀγγελία, a message, but εὐαγγέλιον, the Gospel, the glad tidings of salvation by Jesus Christ, things that “even angels long to look into” and pry into, as the apostle Peter expresses it (1 Pet 1:12). The Lord has also committed to his ministers the administration of the sacraments, which are the seals of his covenant, by which all his precious promises are ratified and confirmed to us. So, as in respect of the rich treasures of God’s word committed to their dispensing they are the Lord’s treasurers, so in respect of the sacraments they are the keepers of his great seal. If these officers are great under mortal princes, what are they under the King of kings?

I have taken the liberty to set out in a few words some of the privileges of the ministers of the Gospel: partly for the comfort and consolation of many of them under the present misery and poverty which they suffer rather than sin against their consciences; and partly to stir up others to give them that double honor which the apostle calls for (1 Tim 5:17), namely, the honor of respect and the honor of maintenance, so that they do not let them sink under their burden, but give them some timely help and relief, suited to their present poverty and needs.

Reason III. Because ministers are most often exposed to sufferings and distresses, and so have most need of relief. The bow of the adversaries of religion is bent most against the teachers and leaders of the people. That word, “Do not fight with anyone, small or great, except the king of Israel” (1 Kgs 22:31), is often changed into, “Do not fight with anyone, small or great, except the prophets of the Lord.” Strike the shepherds, and the sheep will be scattered. Experience tells the world plainly enough who they are that are set in the front of the battle, and who are the first to fall by the power of the adversaries. And who should be most in the eye of charity, but those who are most in the eye of malice?

Besides, for whose sakes is it that ministers are so often brought so low? Is it not for your+ sakes, whose souls are dearer to them than their own wealth? Is it not often on this account: because they will be faithful to you+, and will not keep silent, nor cease to watch over you+, and to warn and instruct you+ from day to day?

Might they not keep themselves more whole if they would hold their peace and leave the devil free to have his will of you+? No doubt it is for your+ sakes that much of their suffering comes on them; and shall they be forsaken by you+? The truth is, on this account it is a piece of justice, as well as a piece of charity, to relieve and help them; and so you+ may do two good works in one: the same alms may be both a work of righteousness and a work of mercy.

Reason IV. Your+ gratitude to God requires a cheerful performance of this duty from you+. For how else can you+ make a fitting return to God for what he has plentifully given you+ than by contributing some of your+ temporal things to those from whom you+ reap so much in spiritual things? The Lord, of his free grace and rich mercy, has abounded toward you+ in these outward things; he has richly given you+ all things to enjoy. Yes, as the psalmist says, he has loaded you+ with his benefits. Now not to return some part of your+ estate to him who has given you+ all that you+ enjoy would be ingratitude of the highest degree. And therefore how much it concerns you+ to put the psalmist’s question often to yourselves+: “How can I repay the Lord for all His benefits to me?” (Ps 116:12). Surely one kindness deserves another. As God has been bountiful to you+, you+ are surely very unworthy if you+ are not bountiful to his own. And how do you+ think he will take it at your+ hands? Will he ever say to you+, “Well done, good and faithful servant! You have been faithful, a good steward of my many gifts”? Or is it all the same to you+ whether he says Well done or not?

And since you+ cannot directly and immediately repay him, who cannot be enriched by us (“my goodness does not extend to You,” Ps 16:2), it will be your+ wisdom to express your+ thankfulness to God by being kind to his poor relations. Now who are nearer to God than his ministers? He has appointed them to stand in his place, to declare his mind to his people. As they are the mouth of the people to God, so they are God’s mouth to the people. They are the messengers of the Lord of hosts, by whose ministry peace is concluded and reconciliation proclaimed between God and man. Surely what kindness you+ show to these, he takes as done to himself (Matt 25:40).

Reason V. Your+ relieving the faithful ministers of Christ may in a sense be said to have something more in it than if you+ showed your+ charity to Christ himself, in his own person, since it is a sign of greater love. It is only an ordinary thing to return kindness to our dearest friends; but to extend our goodwill to their relatives or servants for their sakes is evidence of much greater love. For if we do good to these only on our friends’ account, how much more ready, one would judge, we would be to do it to our friends themselves if they stood in need of our help! And so Christ will look on it: our bounty shown to his ministers he will receive as evidence of our more abundant love to him, which he will by no means forget, nor allow to go unrewarded.

Reason VI. Those who relieve the poor ministers of Christ will have their blessing, the benefit of their prayers to God. They will bless you+ anyway, though you+ have no blessing for them. Though you+ have no alms for them, yet they will have a prayer for you+. But when you+ have refreshed their hearts, you+ may expect their hearts to be the more moved to pray for you+; and this will be a far greater kindness than you+ can give them. Your+ gift cannot be worth as much as their fervent prayers. In this respect it is much better to give than to receive: because he who receives has only a perishing alms, while he who gives receives an abiding blessing, the blessing of prayers.

In this the apostle St. Paul made a large repayment to Onesiphorus for the kindness he showed him in his imprisonment, as you+ may read in 2 Tim 1:16: “May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he has often refreshed me and was unashamed of my chains.” As if he had said, I received much comfort and refreshment from Onesiphorus when I was in prison, and for this I beseech the Father of all mercies to show mercy to him and his, by blessing him and his whole family with all blessings, temporal, spiritual and eternal. And indeed, what blessing can that man lack who has a share in the prayers of many ministers? Their prayers avail to obtain all good things at the hand of God, for others as well as for themselves. Yes, the very work of charity calls for a blessing from God. As the blood of Abel is said to cry to the Lord for a curse or vengeance on Cain, so every act of charity cries to God for a blessing on the charitable. Our very acts of charity in relieving the needs of the poor and refreshing their hearts pray and cry to God for his blessing on us and ours.

Reason VII. Your+ charity to them will be rewarded hereafter with everlasting glory and happiness in the kingdom of heaven. Our Savior himself gives this reason in these words: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward.” By this is meant that surpassing and excellent weight of glory which cannot be expressed by the tongue of men or angels. Yes, the reward of a prophet seems to imply the highest degree of heavenly glory. For it is said in Dan 12:3 that “the wise,” that is, the righteous, who are endowed with true spiritual wisdom, being enlightened by the Spirit of God, “will shine like the brightness of the heavens, but those who lead many to righteousness,” which is the work of prophets, “will shine like the stars forever and ever.”

Now by your+ bounty to the prophets of God you+ may come to share in their reward. So it is your+ own concern to contribute liberally toward their relief. Not that your+ charity to them merits that glorious reward; but because of the promise God has made to all who exercise this charity toward his ministers, the reward will truly be given to them.

The Application

Oh, how the consideration of these things should stir up the hearts of all, especially of those who have a blessing in their hand, an estate to give, to draw out their souls and reach out their hands to supply these needy servants of God! Surely this is a time in which Christ is trying your+ love to him by your+ charity to them. Are you+ not concerned to prove your+ love to Christ? Do you+ not have an opportunity before you+, and a loud call from heaven, to prove it in this way? Can you+ not hear him who once said to Peter (John 21:16), “Do you love Me? … Feed My sheep”? Can you+ not hear the same voice calling to you+, Do you love Me? Feed My shepherds? Surely you are very deaf to the voice of the providences of this day if you do not hear this call. And will you+ prove that you+ have no love to Christ? What else are you+ doing, if you+ let his own starve when you+ have the means to feed them?

Beloved, it is through God’s free grace and rich bounty that you+ enjoy such plenty of outward good things, while many of his ministers are in great want. What you+ have, you+ have received from him. Is it not, then, most just and reasonable that you+ should return some part of your+ estates to God by relieving his ministers, in testimony of your+ love and thankfulness to him for what you+ have? Has God given you+ hundreds and thousands? And will you+ not part with a few pounds or shillings when he calls aloud to you+ for them, as he does now in these days? Though the earth is his, and its fullness, yet (in a sense) he sometimes has need of your+ estates. In Matt 25:35 Christ tells you+ of his needs, and shows you+ how and when he is relieved.

If you+ have any spiritual wisdom to discern times and seasons, you+ may know that Christ now stands in need of your+ helping hand, now that so many of his ministers are in want for the testimony of a good conscience. And should you+ now deny him in his ministers, I truly believe that if Christ were now on earth, as when he first took our nature on him, and asked you+ for relief in his own person, you+ would turn a deaf ear to him.

Though for the present you+ enjoy many blessings, yet how easily he can pluck them out of your+ mouths, and, if you+ will not do your+ duty, thrust you+ down from among the givers to take your+ place among the receivers! Certainly giving away a part is your+ best way to secure the rest, and to season and sanctify it for your+ more comfortable use.

Luke 11:41. Our Savior says, “Give alms of such things as you+ have, and you+ will see that everything is clean for you+”; that is, lawful to be used. The metaphor is taken from the law, by which many things were counted unclean, and so unlawful to use; they were not to be touched or handled. Yes, by the apostle’s inference, “give alms of such things as you+ have, and you+ will see that everything is clean for you+,” he seems to allude to another rite of the law, about firstfruits, tithes, and freewill offerings: by giving these to the Lord, all the rest that the people had was secured, sanctified and made clean. So charitable men are those who may use what they have with the more freedom, quietness and comfort. Who, if he has any desire to be accepted and approved by God, would not have his person, the actions he does, and the things he possesses be clean? Whatever is unclean is odious and abominable in God’s sight. Unclean persons were not allowed to approach God’s sanctuary, nor handle sacred things. If they were not cleansed, they were to be cut off from God’s people (Num 19:20; Lev 7:20). And every unclean thing was an abomination.

This therefore must be a strong persuasion to put into practice the counsel of our Savior, by giving alms of such things as we have, so that everything may be clean, and sanctified, for us. What is clean you+ may use with God’s good leave and allowance (clean things could lawfully be eaten); and where you+ have God’s good leave, you+ may expect his blessing. It is sin to eat where God’s portion is mixed in with it.

The truth is, it is the great mistake of many to think that all their goods are their own, and that they are absolute lords and owners of all they possess. In fact they are stewards rather than lords and owners of this world’s goods; all is the Lord’s. God in his infinite wisdom has committed a greater portion of them to some than to others, yet not to be appropriated to themselves: they must give him his special part, to which his poor have as good a right as the rich have to the rest, except only that the poor must not lay hands on it themselves until you+ put it into their hands. But as they must not take it out of yours+, so you+ must not keep it out of their hands. Therefore Solomon, speaking of the right the poor have to a part of rich men’s estates, says, “Do not withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is within your power to act” (Prov 3:27). So relieving the poor is not only an act of mercy, left to our choice to do or leave undone, but also, as I said before, an act of justice, which we are bound to perform. Hence to give alms and to do righteousness and justice are often put in Scripture one for the other, both meaning the same thing. Therefore the Septuagint has rendered the Hebrew word meaning righteousness in Deuteronomy 24:13 by ἐλεημοσύνην, alms deeds. And in Ps 112:9 it is said, “his righteousness endures forever”; that is, his alms, or his mercifulness, as is clear from the words before it: “He has scattered abroad his gifts to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.” By this it is implied that giving alms is one special branch of that righteousness and justice we owe to our poor neighbors.

And do you dare still hold it in your hand? Will you wrong the Almighty of his right, and rob his poor of their due? If it is nothing to you to be unmerciful, is it nothing either to be a robber? A robber of God? “Will a man rob God?” (Mal 3:8). Does any man dare to be so wicked? How can you not expect that he will make a forcible entry on you, and take what is his own, and seal a writ of ejectment against you, and turn you out of all that you have? Do not look to be long in quiet possession of what you have; but fear that God may take your estate from you, or you from your estate, and give you your portion with Dives, who, because he denied his crumbs to satisfy poor Lazarus’s hunger, was himself denied a drop of cold water to quench his own heat and thirst (Luke 16:24). On these words St. Augustine gives this gloss: Ideo rogans Dives non exauditur in tormentis, quia rogantem pauperem non exaudivit. Therefore Dives was not heard when he prayed in torments, because he did not listen to the poor man who begged of him when he was on the earth. Aug. Serm. De Divite.

Let me add a few stirring words, to press home what has been said, by the following questions.

Question 1. Now at last, what do you think of mercy and bounty to the poor?

1. Is there not an excellence in it? Oh, how much of God there is in it! There is faith in it. The man who will cast his bread upon the waters, is it not a sure sign that he believes God, who has said that it will be returned to him? There is the love of God in it. “If anyone … sees his brother in need, but shuts up his compassion from him, how can the love of God dwell in him?” And the man who opens his heart and draws out his soul to God’s hungry ones, who can deny that the love of God dwells in that man? It is the image of God’s goodness. God is a merciful God, and his mercy is his glory; and this glory of God shines out in his merciful servants. There is self-denial in it. Self would keep all; the flesh would hold back; it cannot spare anything for God. It is a sign that self is laid low, that the flesh is kept under, that the cause of God is the ruling cause, when self is not allowed to keep back whatever God will have. Is there so much of God in mercifulness, and is there not an excellence in it?

2. Is there not a necessity of it? Will the merciless ever obtain mercy? Can you hope for mercy if you will show no mercy?

Question 2. What do you think of yourself? Are you merciful, or merciless? How do you find it? Is your heart open? Is your compassion open? Or is it still shut up? Do you feel that heart of yours inclined and resolved to open your hands, and to disperse, and that liberally, the good things you have received, as a good steward of the manifold gifts of God? Or do you still feel that the door is shut, that your heart is hardened against showing kindness to the Lord? Give your plain judgment: what do you think? Are you a merciful man, or merciless? And if merciless, how do you hope to obtain mercy?

Question 3. What do you think of your worldly goods?

(1.) Are they not your talents, committed to you for your Lord’s use? Must you not give him an account of how they have been laid out? Will it be a comfortable account when you must bring in your bill: so much for your pride, so much for your appetite, or all hoarded up for your covetousness, and nothing, or only a little, for God?

(2.) Are they worth more than treasures in heaven? Is it more to your advantage to be rich in this world’s goods than to be rich in good works? Do you judge in good earnest that laying up treasures on earth is better management than laying up in store for yourself a good foundation for the time to come?

Question 4. What do you think of the state of many of the servants of God in this age? Are there none in want? None in distress? What, neither among ministers nor among Christians? Are they all provided for? Do not many of them eat the bread and drink the water of affliction? Are they not in great straits and very short of things? Only inquire after their condition, and you will find it so. Are you one of those who do not care how it goes with the poor friends of Christ? Are they not worth inquiring and looking after? Or at least, is not he worthy whose they are and whom they serve? Is not Christ worthy, for whose sake you should show kindness to his own? How will he take your neglect of them? Remember that word: “Whatever you+ did not do for … these, you+ did not do for Me” (Matt 25:45).

Question 5. What will you do from now on? What will be the outcome of these few words written for your learning? What are you resolved on: mercy, or cruelty? Consult your own heart. Do not lay this little book aside until you have come to a resolution one way or the other, either to accept or to reject this counsel, which is offered to you in the name of the Lord for your good. Oh, show yourself a man in whose soul Christ has a claim, and so great a claim that you will do anything at his word: pity at his word, relieve at his word, give, lend, feed, clothe, refresh the hearts of his needy ones. Let your soul say, Lord, at your word I will do it. Here is my bread, and my flesh, and my money; command what you will of it, I will not say no to you. You have given me a large portion, and every one of your servants whom you appoint to receive it will have his part; for your sake, Lord, they will have it. I am yours, and all that I have is yours. Show me your will: how much, and how often, and where, and to whom I am to give it; and through the grace of God, there it will go.

Friend, will you say this? Will you, in the presence of the Lord, come to this gracious resolution? Or can you still find it in your heart to deny your Lord, and go on being as hard-hearted and close-handed as you used to be? Do not dare to say, Lord, my goods are my own, I owe you nothing. Dread such thoughts, that however much you have, the servants of Christ will be none the better for it.

Once again consider: you are put to this choice, either to accept the counsel of Christ or to reject it. Which of the two will you do? If you do not resolve on mercy and liberality, you reject the word of the Lord; and if you reject his word, you reject the Lord, and in doing so you say, He will be no Lord of mine. But if you accept it, then go and do accordingly. Let the hunger and the thirst and the nakedness, the needs and distresses of his servants, feel in the relief they receive from you that you are a man to whom the Lord has not spoken in vain. Let them feel it now, and let them feel it constantly: this year, and the next year, and the next, as long as they have need to receive and you have it by you to give. Do this, and may the Lord accept you; may he remember all your offerings and accept all your sacrifices; the Lord answer you in the day of your trouble; the name of the God of Jacob defend you; the Lord grant you according to your own heart and fulfill all your counsel; the Lord remember you with the favor he bears to his children, and visit you with his salvation.
